title: Research
text:
Research
  Mathematical structure, computation and applications
  My research connects rigorous analysis with algorithms and applied models. It has developed through three main themes: optimisation and inverse problems, PDEs and materials, and statistical modelling for decision-making.



  11peer-reviewed journal articles
  3major research themes
  12invited research talks
  UK · Austria · Italyinternational research network



  
    Research approach
    From theory to methods that can be tested
  
  I am interested in problems where structure matters: data may be incomplete, systems may evolve over time, or the quantity of interest may not be directly observable. I use mathematical analysis to understand the problem, optimisation and statistics to construct methods, and computation to test their behaviour. The result may be a theorem, an algorithm, a model or a decision rule—but the underlying aim is the same: reliable conclusions from difficult information.



  01
  
    Optimisation · Inverse problems · Imaging
    Recovering dynamic structure from incomplete data
  
  
    During my postdoctoral research at the University of Graz, I helped develop a framework for reconstructing time-dependent sources from noisy, severely undersampled measurements. The work combines optimal-transport regularisation with generalized conditional-gradient methods, allowing moving sources to be represented sparsely and updated through interpretable trajectories.
    The programme developed from functional analysis and well-posedness theory to convergence analysis, algorithm design and numerical experiments for dynamic MRI and Fourier measurements.
    
      QuestionHow can motion be reconstructed when each time point contains only a small and noisy fraction of the required data?
      ContributionDynamic regularisation models, sparse optimisation algorithms and convergence guarantees.
      MethodsOptimal transport, convex analysis, conditional gradients, measure-valued optimisation and numerical simulation.
    
    Foundations of Computational Mathematics →Code →
  



  02
  
    PDEs · Variational methods · Materials
    Explaining macroscopic structure from microscopic defects
  
  
    My doctoral research studied how dislocations and phase geometry influence the large-scale behaviour of crystalline materials. I developed and analysed variational models for semi-coherent interfaces, grain boundaries and two-phase composites, connecting microscopic defect mechanisms with emergent structures.
    This work strengthened my ability to move between physical intuition, precise mathematical formulation and asymptotic analysis—skills that remain useful far beyond materials science.
    
      QuestionHow do local defects and competing energies create observable material patterns?
      ContributionMacroscopic limit models for dislocations, polycrystals and interface structure.
      MethodsPDEs, calculus of variations, Γ-convergence, geometric measure theory and convex integration.
    
    SIAM Journal on Mathematical Analysis →Related publications →
  



  03
  
    Statistical learning · Sports · Decisions
    Interpretable models for performance and strategy
  
  
    At the University of Hull I developed a research strand in statistical sports modelling, closely connected to teaching and student supervision. The Formula 1 work separates driver ability from constructor strength through a time-rank duality, while the curling work combines econometric estimation, Markov modelling and simulation to quantify hammer advantage and derive strategic conditions for blanking an end.
    These projects show how simple, transparent models can produce useful benchmarks and decisions when data are limited and effects are confounded.
    
      QuestionHow can performance and strategic effects be separated from unequal conditions?
      ContributionInterpretable probabilistic models, estimated effects, simulations and explicit decision rules.
      MethodsRegression, probability models, likelihood, Markov chains, simulation and model comparison.

title: Sparsity by design: building solutions one atom at a time
text:
Optimisation
  
  A plain-language tour of our Mathematical Programming paper on fully-corrective generalized conditional gradient methods — with the whole idea worked out on the lasso, where you can see every moving part.
  
    
      Author
      Silvio Fanzon
    
    
      Published
      Jan. 1, 2025
        
      Resources
      Open-access paperGitHub
Companion post to Asymptotic linear convergence of fully-corrective generalized conditional gradient methods (Bredies, Carioni, Fanzon & Walter, Mathematical Programming, 2024 — open access). The linked Python repository is a pedagogical lasso implementation created to explain and test the paper’s ideas; it is not the original research code used to produce the theoretical paper. Code and experiments: github.com/sfanzon/sparse-gcg-paper-explainer.

title: Sparsity by design: building solutions one atom at a time
section: The problem, without the Banach spaces
text:
The problem, without the Banach spaces
A huge amount of modern applied maths boils down to problems of the shape
\[\min_u \;\; \underbrace{F(Ku)}_{\text{fit the data}} \; + \; \underbrace{R(u)}_{\text{keep it simple}}\]
Reconstructing an MRI image from too few measurements, locating point sources from sensor data, training a sparse regression model — all instances. The regularizer \(R\) encodes a preference for simple solutions, and for a large family of regularizers “simple” means sparse: the solution is a combination of a handful of elementary building blocks, or atoms.
Here is the key geometric fact the paper is built on. The atoms are not arbitrary — they are the extremal points of the unit ball of \(R\): the “corners” of the ball, the points that cannot be written as averages of other points in it. And there’s a classical lemma that makes them algorithmically accessible: a linear function on a ball is always maximised at an extremal point. So if you can maximise linear functions over the ball — one cheap operation — you can discover atoms one at a time.
Our algorithm, FC-GCG (fully-corrective generalized conditional gradient), does exactly that, alternating two steps:

Insertion. Look at the current residual, ask “which single atom correlates best with what’s still unexplained?” — a linear problem, solved at an extremal point — and add that atom to your working set.
Full correction. Re-optimise the objective over combinations of only the atoms collected so far. This is a low-dimensional convex problem — cheap, because your working set is small — and it also discards atoms that turn out to be useless.

Two properties fall out immediately. Iterates are sparse at every iteration, by construction — sparsity is not something you converge towards, it’s the data structure. And the algorithm can stop with a certificate: if no atom correlates with the residual above the threshold set by \(R\), the optimality conditions hold exactly.
What the paper proves: the method always converges at the classical Frank–Wolfe rate \(O(1/k)\), and — this is the hard part, and the reason the paper is 68 pages — under a natural non-degeneracy condition on the dual variable, convergence is eventually linear: the error shrinks geometrically. The proof lifts the problem to a space where the atoms become coordinates, which is also a decent mental model for the algorithm itself.

title: Sparsity by design: building solutions one atom at a time
section: The whole idea on one example: the lasso
text:
The whole idea on one example: the lasso
Everything above lives in infinite-dimensional Banach spaces in the paper. But you can watch every gear turn in the most familiar sparse problem there is — the lasso in \(\mathbb{R}^n\):
\[\min_x \;\tfrac12 \lVert Ax - b\rVert^2 + \lambda \lVert x \rVert_1 .\]
The unit ball of \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_1\) is the cross-polytope, and its extremal points are simply the \(2n\) signed coordinate vectors \(\pm e_i\). So the abstract algorithm becomes something you could explain to a first-year student:

Insertion: compute the correlations \(p = A^\top(b - Ax_k)\) of each column with the residual; pick the column with the largest \(|p_i|\). If \(\max_i |p_i| \le \lambda\): stop — you are exactly optimal.
Full correction: solve the lasso restricted to the columns picked so far — a problem in 5, 10, 15 variables instead of \(n\) — and drop columns whose coefficient is zero.

If this reminds you of matching pursuit: yes — FC-GCG is the convex, certificate-carrying relative of greedy methods, and in the general Banach setting it’s the algorithmic engine behind “grid-free” approaches to inverse problems.

title: Sparsity by design: building solutions one atom at a time
section: Racing it: FC-GCG vs Frank–Wolfe vs gradient descent
text:
Racing it: FC-GCG vs Frank–Wolfe vs gradient descent
The natural baselines are vanilla Frank–Wolfe (same insertion oracle, but instead of re-optimising it just averages the new atom in with step size \(2/(k+2)\)) and proximal gradient descent (ISTA, plus its accelerated version FISTA) — the workhorse “gradient descent for sparse problems”. We race them on a lasso with \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{300\times 5000}\) and an 11-atom solution:



Objective suboptimality vs iteration. FC-GCG inserts 11 atoms, then stops at iteration 12 with an exact optimality certificate.


The qualitative gap is exactly what the theory predicts. Frank–Wolfe’s averaging step is what caps it at \(O(1/k)\) — it keeps diluting good atoms with step-size bookkeeping and zig-zags near the solution. ISTA converges linearly but slowly. FC-GCG does something the plot renders almost violent: one insertion per solution atom, then done, at machine precision — the “fully-corrective” step means an atom, once found, is used optimally forever.
There’s a second story in the support size of the iterates:



Support size along the run. Proximal-gradient iterates are dense early and sparsify late; FC-GCG never exceeds the solution’s sparsity.


ISTA and FISTA wander through hundreds of nonzeros before settling; FC-GCG never holds more atoms than the answer needs. In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) that’s an aesthetic point. In the infinite-dimensional problems the paper actually targets, it’s the whole point — off a grid, a “dense iterate” doesn’t even exist, while “a list of a few atoms” is a perfectly good data structure.

title: Sparsity by design: building solutions one atom at a time
text:
Where it pays: high dimensions
All four methods pay the same \(O(mn)\) per iteration — one sweep of the data to compute a gradient or dual variable. So wall-clock time is decided by how many iterations you need, and FC-GCG’s count is essentially the number of atoms in the solution, independent of the ambient dimension:



Wall time to solve to relative accuracy \(10^{-8}\), dimension up to \(n = 200{,}000\). Open markers: iteration cap hit before reaching the tolerance.


At \(n = 200{,}000\) the difference is orders of magnitude — not because FC-GCG’s iterations are cheaper (they’re marginally more expensive — each includes a tiny inner solve), but because it takes ~15 of them where the baselines take thousands. Concretely, at \(n=200{,}000\): 1 second for FC-GCG versus 96–106 seconds for FW/ISTA/FISTA — with all three baselines still short of the target accuracy when their iteration caps hit. This is the regime the method was designed for: in our companion work on dynamic MRI, the “dimension” is a continuum — atoms are curves of moving point sources — and building solutions atom-by-atom is not an optimisation trick but the only viable representation.
Fine print, in fairness. The lasso instance here is deliberately easy — well-conditioned Gaussian designs satisfy the paper’s non-degeneracy assumptions comfortably, which is what makes the convergence so clean. And specialised lasso solvers (coordinate descent with screening rules) are also very fast on this problem; the comparison above is between general-purpose first-order schemes, which are the ones that generalise to the measure-space setting.

title: Sparsity by design: building solutions one atom at a time
text:
The three ideas worth stealing
Even if you never touch a Banach space, the design principles travel:

Match your data structure to your prior. If you believe the answer is sparse, iterate over lists of atoms, not dense vectors.
Certificates beat convergence. A stopping rule of the form “no atom correlates above \(\lambda\)” is an exact optimality proof, not a heuristic tolerance.
Spend compute where it compounds. The fully-corrective step looks expensive per iteration but slashes the iteration count — the classic trade of a cheap outer loop for a smart inner one.

title: Who’s actually the best F1 driver?
text:
Statistical modelling
  
  Companion code and technical walkthrough for our joint paper on separating driver performance from car advantage with time–rank duality.
  
    
      Author
      Silvio Fanzon
    
    
      Published
      Mar. 18, 2024
        
      Resources
      Paper PDFJournal articleGitHub

title: Who’s actually the best F1 driver?
text:
The problem
When Max Verstappen wins a race, how much of that is Max — and how much is the Red Bull?
This is a hard identification problem. Driver and car are tightly confounded because a driver only competes in their own team’s machinery. Earlier econometric studies often pool many seasons and exploit drivers changing teams. That is valuable historically, but it is less helpful when the question is: who is outperforming their car now?
Our paper shows how to reach an informative comparison using one season of public race results and the betting odds for one later race. The key is a bridge between two ways of modelling the same race.

title: Who’s actually the best F1 driver?
text:
Two models, one bridge
The time model. Treat each car’s finishing time as exponentially distributed, \(T_i \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_i)\). Larger \(\lambda_i\) means a faster latent race time. The resulting win probability is exactly
\[
\Pr(\text{car }j\text{ wins})=
\frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n}.
\]
This is mathematically clean and easy to calibrate to bookmaker probabilities, but complete finishing times are usually unavailable because lapped cars do not cover the full race distance.
The rank model. Finishing positions are public, so model each rank as Gaussian, \(r_i\sim N(\mu_i,\sigma^2)\). The model again gives a closed-form win probability.
Time–rank duality. Equating the two win probabilities translates the bookmaker information from the time model into expected finishing positions in the rank model. The analysis gets the tractability of the first model and the observability of the second.

How the analysis works

This is the modelling pipeline, not page navigation. The first two stages translate market information into expected ranks; the final two learn and apply a historical benchmark.



Input2023 race oddsConvert bookmaker odds into adjusted win probabilities.


TranslationTime–rank dualityTurn those probabilities into expected finishing positions.


Benchmark2022 season modelEstimate constructor effects and a conservative teammate threshold.


DecisionTeammate comparisonFlag expected-rank gaps that exceed the car-only benchmark.








Two datasets have different jobs. The 2022 results estimate the historical benchmark. The 2023 Qatar odds produce the expected ranks to which that benchmark is applied. Keeping those stages separate is essential.

title: Who’s actually the best F1 driver?
section: First look: cars dominate the raw results
text:
First look: cars dominate the raw results
The first picture is deliberately descriptive. Each point is a driver’s average finishing position over the 25 recorded races and sprints in 2022, with teammates placed side by side.



Each driver’s observed average finishing position in 2022, grouped by constructor. Lower positions are better.


The large jumps between constructors show immediately why car quality cannot be ignored. Red Bull, Mercedes and Ferrari occupy a very different part of the plot from the back of the grid. The smaller gaps within each constructor suggest an additional driver-level effect — but these raw averages are not the final comparison.






NoteShow the base-R code for this figure





#' Figure 3: each driver's observed 2022 average, grouped by constructor
#'
#' This is a descriptive plot of the historical dataset. It is useful for
#' seeing the large constructor differences and the within-team spreads, but
#' it is not the Section 5 driver-versus-car calculation. Section 5 uses the
#' 2023 odds-implied expected ranks shown in Figure 4.
#'
#' @param driver_table output from driver_average_table()
#' @param file output PNG path
plot_driver_vs_team <- function(
    driver_table,
    file = "figures/03_driver_vs_team.png"
) {
  team_order <- c(
    "RedBull", "Mercedes", "Ferrari", "McLaren", "Alpine",
    "AstonMartin", "Haas", "AlphaTauri", "AlfaRomeo", "Williams"
  )
  axis_labels <- c(
    "RedBull", "Mercedes", "Ferrari", "Mclaren", "Alpine",
    "AstonMartin", "Haas", "AlfaTauri", "AlfaRomeo", "Williams"
  )

  dt <- driver_table
  dt$constructor <- factor(dt$constructor, levels = team_order)
  dt <- dt[order(dt$constructor, dt$second_driver), , drop = FALSE]

  teammate_number <- ave(
    seq_len(nrow(dt)),
    dt$constructor,
    FUN = seq_along
  )
  x <- as.numeric(dt$constructor) + ifelse(teammate_number == 1, -0.15, 0.15)
  last_name <- sub("([A-Z][a-z]+)([A-Z].*)", "\\2", dt$driver)

  # Small label adjustments keep neighbouring names readable while preserving
  # the original plot's side-by-side structure.
  y_shift <- rep(0.48, nrow(dt))
  y_shift[last_name %in% c("Russel", "Leclerc", "Bottas")] <- -0.48
  y_shift[last_name %in% c("Magnussen", "Schumacher", "Tsunoda", "Guanyu")] <- 0.62

  png(file, width = 1000, height = 680, res = 130)
  op <- par(mar = c(7, 5, 3, 1))
  on.exit({
    par(op)
    dev.off()
  }, add = TRUE)

  plot(
    x,
    dt$avg_position,
    pch = 19,
    col = "#cc0164",
    cex = 1.3,
    xaxt = "n",
    xlab = "",
    ylab = "average finishing position (2022 season)",
    xlim = c(min(x) - 0.4, max(x) + 0.3),
    ylim = c(min(dt$avg_position) - 0.8, max(dt$avg_position) + 1.3),
    main = paste(
      "Each driver's actual average position, by team",
      "(teammates plotted side by side)",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  )

  axis(1, at = seq_along(team_order), labels = axis_labels, las = 2)
  for (i in seq_along(team_order)) {
    abline(v = i, col = "gray90", lty = 3)
  }
  points(x, dt$avg_position, pch = 19, col = "#cc0164", cex = 1.3)
  text(
    x,
    dt$avg_position + y_shift,
    labels = last_name,
    cex = 0.65
  )

  invisible(file)
}

title: Who’s actually the best F1 driver?
section: Estimate the car effect rather than eyeballing it
text:
Estimate the car effect rather than eyeballing it
The regression uses all 500 driver-race observations. It explains finishing position using constructor indicators while retaining a second-driver indicator. The constructor coefficients below are relative to the omitted baseline teams; negative values mean a better expected finishing position.



Estimated constructor effects from the selected 2022 regression, with 95% confidence intervals.


The ordering matches the intuitive picture, but the model makes the comparison explicit. Red Bull has the largest estimated advantage, followed by Mercedes and Ferrari. The estimated second-driver penalty is only \(0.216\) positions and is statistically uncertain; its 95% confidence interval is \((-0.581,\ 1.013)\).
The upper endpoint, 1.013 positions, becomes a conservative benchmark. A later within-team expected-rank gap above this value is larger than the historical car-and-teammate pattern can comfortably explain.

#' Figure 2: constructor effects from the selected 2022 regression
#'
#' @param model fitted model returned by select_models()$stepwise
#' @param file output PNG path
plot_team_effects <- function(
    model,
    file = "figures/02_team_effects.png"
) {
  tab <- regression_table(model)
  model_terms <- c(
    "RedBull", "Mercedes", "Ferrari", "McLaren", "Alpine", "AstonMartin"
  )
  display_names <- c(
    RedBull = "RedBull",
    Mercedes = "Mercedes",
    Ferrari = "Ferrari",
    McLaren = "Mclaren",
    Alpine = "Alpine",
    AstonMartin = "AstonMartin"
  )

  rows <- match(model_terms, tab$term)
  est <- tab$estimate[rows]
  se <- tab$std_error[rows]
  names(est) <- model_terms
  names(se) <- model_terms
  ord <- order(est)

  png(file, width = 950, height = 650, res = 130)
  op <- par(mar = c(5, 9, 3, 1))
  on.exit({
    par(op)
    dev.off()
  }, add = TRUE)

  y <- barplot(
    est[ord],
    horiz = TRUE,
    names.arg = unname(display_names[names(est)[ord]]),
    las = 1,
    col = "#1f3a5f",
    border = NA,
    xlim = c(min(est - 2 * se), 1),
    xlab = "effect on average finishing position (vs. baseline teams)",
    main = paste(
      "Team effect, 2022 season",
      "(negative = better average finishing position)",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  )

  arrows(
    est[ord] - 1.96 * se[ord], y,
    est[ord] + 1.96 * se[ord], y,
    angle = 90,
    code = 3,
    length = 0.05,
    col = "black"
  )
  abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray40")

section: Apply the benchmark to the 2023 Qatar odds
text:
Apply the benchmark to the 2023 Qatar odds
Bookmaker odds for the Qatar Grand Prix are converted into implied win probabilities, adjusted for the bookmaker margin, and translated through the duality into expected finishing ranks. The analysis then compares the two expected ranks within each constructor.



Odds-implied teammate gaps for the 2023 Qatar Grand Prix. The dashed line is the 1.013-position historical threshold.


Two drivers — and only two — clear the threshold:

Max Verstappen versus Sergio Perez: an expected-position gap of about 7.669;
Fernando Alonso versus Lance Stroll: an expected-position gap of about 2.403.

The remaining within-team gaps are below 1.013. In the language of the model, Verstappen and Alonso are the two drivers whose market-implied advantage over their teammates is too large to attribute to the car-only benchmark learned from 2022.






NoteShow the base-R code for this figure





#' Figure 4: odds-implied teammate gaps compared with the historical threshold
#'
#' @param gaps output from teammate_gaps()
#' @param threshold upper endpoint from second_driver_ci()
#' @param file output PNG path
plot_teammate_gaps <- function(
    gaps,
    threshold,
    file = "figures/04_teammate_gaps.png"
) {
  gaps <- gaps[order(-gaps$gap), , drop = FALSE]
  labels <- paste0(gaps$leading_driver, "  (", gaps$team, ")")
  cols <- ifelse(gaps$outperforms_car, "#C8102E", "grey65")

  png(file, width = 1800, height = 1050, res = 180)
  op <- par(mar = c(5, 15, 3, 2), xpd = NA)
  on.exit({
    par(op)
    dev.off()
  }, add = TRUE)

  bp <- barplot(
    rev(gaps$gap),
    horiz = TRUE,
    col = rev(cols),
    border = NA,
    names.arg = rev(labels),
    las = 1,
    cex.names = 0.78,
    xlim = c(0, max(gaps$gap) * 1.08),
    xlab = "Expected-position gap to team-mate (odds-implied)",
    main = "Which drivers outperform their car?"
  )

  abline(v = threshold, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  text(
    threshold,
    max(bp),
    pos = 4,
    cex = 0.8,
    labels = sprintf("car-only threshold = %.3f", threshold)
  )

  invisible(file)
}









What this does not say: the raw 2022 teammate averages are not tested against the threshold. They are useful context, while the final comparison uses the 2023 odds-implied expected ranks. The technical walkthrough documents the distinction and reproduces the relevant tables and checks.

title: Who’s actually the best F1 driver?
section: From a paper to a reproducible analysis

title: Who’s actually the best F1 driver?
text:
Responsible interpretation
“Outperforming the car” is a model-based statement, not a direct measurement of immutable driver ability. It combines a threshold estimated from 2022 with information embedded in one race’s 2023 betting market. The conclusion depends on assumptions including independent exponential race times, a Gaussian rank approximation, common rank variance and the information contained in bookmaker odds.
The strength of the project is not that those assumptions are invisible; it is that the full chain from data to claim is explicit, reproducible and open to scrutiny.

title: Who’s actually the best F1 driver?
text:
Why I like this project

Tractability becomes useful information. Choosing models with exact win probabilities makes the time–rank bridge possible.
Constraints reduce the data burden. The fact that ranks always sum to \(n(n+1)/2\) identifies a parameter that would otherwise need estimating.
A sharp question beats brute force. Careful structure extracts a current-season comparison from far less historical data than a large pooled model.

The method extends beyond motorsport to any setting where you observe rankings but reason about latent performance — horse racing, esports, even recruitment funnels.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
section: The first principle: one source of truth
text:
The first principle: one source of truth
The system starts with one canonical file:
AI-RULES.md
This contains the complete rule set.
It is deliberately vendor-independent. It should describe how I want an AI to work, not how a particular product implements custom instructions.
That matters because platforms change. Model names change. Interfaces change. Limits change.
The rules should survive all of that.
A typical repository looks like this:
AI-Rules/
├── README.md
├── AI-RULES.md
├── AI-RULES-CORE.md
└── presets/
    ├── MATH-RESEARCH.md
    ├── CODING.md
    ├── EDITING.md
    └── LONG-CHATS.md
The master file is canonical.
The other files are deployment subsets, not independent rulebooks.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
section: Why not just one file everywhere?
text:
Why not just one file everywhere?
I initially wanted to paste the entire rule file into every AI system.
That is attractive because it avoids drift.
But there are practical reasons to keep a master file plus smaller deployment sets:

Persistent instruction fields may have character limits.
Coding rules are irrelevant in many ordinary conversations.
Some systems have global instructions and separate project instructions.
Coding agents may read repository files such as AGENTS.md.
Local models may receive rules through a system prompt.
Different tasks benefit from different subsets of the same master rules.

So the design became:
AI-RULES.md       # canonical master
AI-RULES-CORE.md  # rules that should apply almost everywhere

presets/
  MATH-RESEARCH.md
  CODING.md
  EDITING.md
  LONG-CHATS.md
The important constraint is:

The presets should be extracts from the master, not rewritten interpretations of it.

If the wording in a preset drifts from the master, the system becomes unreliable.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
text:
The global rules
The global rules are mostly about information density and epistemic discipline.

Result first
The answer should begin with the conclusion, not a long preamble.
This does not mean removing reasoning. It means the reasoning comes after the user knows what the answer is.


Concise but complete
The goal is not a rigid word limit.
The better rule is:

Use the shortest answer that is still complete.

That avoids two bad extremes:

unnecessarily long answers;
artificially short answers that omit useful points.

The aim is high information density.


Challenge assumptions, but do not be pedantic
A useful AI should notice when an important assumption is questionable.
It should not derail every discussion over minor technicalities.
The distinction is simple:

challenge assumptions that materially affect the conclusion;
ignore trivial imperfections unless they matter.



Label the status of claims
For technical work, it is useful to distinguish:

Proved / verified
Numerically checked
Plausible
Speculative

This is especially valuable during brainstorming, where a good idea can easily sound more established than it really is.


Preserve follow-up ideas without letting them take over
Long conversations often grow because every interesting branch gets explored immediately.
A better rule is:

When several follow-up ideas arise, put them under short headings. Explore each enough to explain the idea, why it matters, and the likely next step, but do not fully develop every branch automatically.

For example:


Follow-up — Alternative model
Plausible. A different probabilistic model may remove an unrealistic assumption in the current approach. It is worth testing if the original model fails validation.


Follow-up — Exact computation
Numerically checked. A simulation currently estimates the quantity, but an exact integral may be possible and would make a good validation exercise.
The idea is preserved, but the main answer stays focused.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
text:
Rules for research and literature
The research rules are separate because source handling is a different problem from mathematical reasoning.
The main principles are:

prefer primary sources;
cite the main nontrivial external claims;
show disagreements in the literature instead of smoothing them away;
separate:

what the source says;
the AI’s interpretation;
proposed extensions.


That last distinction is easy to lose.
An AI can move very quickly from:

“The paper proves X”

into:

“This suggests Y”

and then into:

“Therefore Z is probably true”

without making the transitions explicit.
The rule system forces those layers apart.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
text:
Rules for coding
The coding rules grew out of a common agentic-workflow problem: powerful coding agents are useful, but it is easy to overuse them.
The default rule is:

Prefer the smallest clean change that solves the task.

But there is an important exception:

If the local fix would become hacky, suggest a refactor instead.

This avoids two opposite failure modes:

refactoring an entire codebase for a tiny change;
stacking patches until the code becomes fragile.

Other coding rules include:

explain important changes, not every line;
do not change architecture, visual identity, or naming conventions without asking;
read project guidance first (AGENTS.md, README.md, DESIGN.md, etc.);
after an edit, report concisely what changed and where.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
section: Let the AI choose the model tier
text:
Let the AI choose the model tier
One of the most useful rules concerns coding agents.
If a chat model generates a prompt for a coding agent, it should also say which class of model is appropriate for the task.
The user should not have to guess whether the task is easy or hard.
The rule is:

Recommend the cheapest or lightest model likely to complete the task reliably.

The recommendation should be:

based on the generated task itself;
vendor-neutral;
updated as model availability changes;
explicit about reasoning level or effort when useful.

A stronger model should only be recommended when it is genuinely justified.
This is a useful antidote to a common tendency: always reaching for the most expensive model because of fear that a cheaper one might miss something.
A better workflow is:
chat model
   ↓
understand task
   ↓
draft coding-agent prompt
   ↓
estimate task difficulty
   ↓
recommend suitable model tier
   ↓
run agent
This keeps the expensive models for the work that actually needs them.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
text:
Rules for editing existing files
Document editing caused one of the biggest sources of drift in my workflow.
Repeatedly asking an AI to “update” a document can quietly turn into repeated rewriting.
After a few iterations, the document may be internally consistent but no longer faithful to the original discussion.
So the editing rules are deliberately conservative.

Treat the current file as canonical
Unless a rewrite is explicitly requested, the current file is the baseline.


“Add” does not mean “rewrite”
If I ask to add material, the AI should add material.
It should not reinterpret the request as permission to restructure or rewrite existing sections.


“Merge” is ambiguous
A merge may mean:

append;
reconcile;
deduplicate;
restructure;
preserve both versions.

The AI should clarify which interpretation is intended.


Ask before rewriting older sections
If new material creates a contradiction with existing text, that is not permission to silently fix the old section.
The AI should flag the conflict and ask before changing it.


Keep a concise changelog
After substantial edits, the AI should say what changed and where.
This makes file evolution much easier to audit.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
text:
Rules for long chats
Long chats are useful.
They are also dangerous.
They encourage the illusion that the entire conversation remains perfectly available and coherent forever.
In practice, long conversations can become difficult for both the user and the model to manage.
The rules therefore include a small amount of conversational self-management.

Keep the main thread focused
Side branches go under Follow-up ideas rather than expanding automatically.


Occasionally suggest a fresh chat
The key word is occasionally.
A reminder every ten messages would become irritating.
The AI should only suggest a fresh chat when the current conversation has genuinely become broad enough that context confusion is likely.


Provide a handoff first
Before suggesting a new chat, produce a compact handoff:
Current question
Established conclusions
Open questions
Useful follow-ups
That gives the next chat a clean starting point.


Be honest about context loss
A long-chat summary should not automatically be described as perfectly faithful.
For technical work, the AI should distinguish between:

extracted from visible/current context;
reconstructed from compressed context;
uncertain and needing verification against the source chat.

That is much safer than pretending to remember everything.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
section: Canonical notes should override conversational memory
text:
Canonical notes should override conversational memory
This rule connects AI behaviour to external notes.
If a project has a canonical Markdown file and the AI remembers something different, the AI should say so.
The rule is:

Canonical project notes/files override conversational memory. If there is a conflict, identify it explicitly and use the canonical source unless instructed otherwise.

This avoids silent drift.
It also makes external notes useful without requiring an elaborate knowledge-management system.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
text:
Chat is not a notebook
This was the larger lesson.
A chat is excellent for:

asking questions;
exploring ideas;
checking calculations;
generating alternatives;
debugging;
drafting.

It is not ideal as the permanent record of a project.
That does not mean every conversation needs to become a formal note.
A much lighter distinction is enough:

Chat explores. Notes preserve.

A project note might contain only:
# Project

## Current

## Decisions

## Ideas

## Next
The point is not to create a complicated personal knowledge system.
The point is to avoid making the chat history the only place where important decisions live.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
text:
Deployment across tools
The same rules can be deployed differently depending on the platform.
A practical pattern is:
Ordinary chat
= CORE

Maths / research
= CORE + MATH-RESEARCH

Coding
= CORE + CODING

Editing a technical document
= CORE + MATH-RESEARCH + EDITING

Long mathematical brainstorming
= CORE + MATH-RESEARCH + LONG-CHATS
The canonical master remains unchanged.
The deployment layer adapts the rules to the tool.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
text:
General chat assistants
For a general chat system with persistent custom instructions:
global instructions
= AI-RULES-CORE.md
For a project-specific context:
project instructions
= CORE
+ relevant presets
+ project-specific constraints
The exact interface varies between products.
The important point is architectural:

Platform settings are deployments of the rules, not the source of truth.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
text:
Coding agents
Coding agents often support repository-level instruction files.
For example:
AGENTS.md
can contain project-specific coding rules.
A sensible split is:
global agent instructions
= CORE

repository instructions
= CODING
+ project-specific constraints
This is preferable to hiding behavioural expectations inside prompts generated ad hoc each time.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
section: Why version control is worth it
text:
Why version control is worth it
The rules are small, but important.
That makes them an unusually good candidate for Git.
A simple repository is enough:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial AI rules"
Then rule changes become explicit:
git add .
git commit -m "Refine long-chat handling"
This gives useful capabilities:

see exactly what changed;
revert a bad rule;
compare versions;
synchronize across machines;
keep platform-specific deployments reproducible.

It also creates a healthy discipline:

Change the master intentionally, then deploy the change.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
text:
The final architecture
The complete system is deliberately small:
AI-Rules/
├── README.md
├── AI-RULES.md
├── AI-RULES-CORE.md
└── presets/
    ├── MATH-RESEARCH.md
    ├── CODING.md
    ├── EDITING.md
    └── LONG-CHATS.md
And conceptually:
                 AI-RULES.md
                      │
                 source of truth
                      │
          ┌───────────┴───────────┐
          │                       │
        CORE                   presets
          │                       │
          └───────────┬───────────┘
                      │
                deployment layer
                      │
       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
       │              │              │
   chat models    coding agents   local models
The project knowledge system is separate:
Project note
├── Current
├── Decisions
├── Ideas
└── Next
The two systems interact, but should not be confused.

title: A Portable Rule System for Working with AI
What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
text:
AI is extraordinarily good at producing work.
That is not the same thing as being good at deciding what work should be done.
I learned this distinction while using AI to inspect and improve a technical project. The initial task was narrow: understand the existing code, identify genuine problems, and make a small number of justified improvements.
The tools were capable. They could read an unfamiliar repository, inspect numerical methods, generate tests, reorganise experiments, rewrite documentation, and propose new abstractions remarkably quickly.
That was also the problem.
A small issue gradually turned into a much larger intervention. Each individual change sounded reasonable. More validation sounded better than less. More explicit APIs sounded safer. A unified experimental framework sounded cleaner. Stronger numerical safeguards sounded more rigorous.
But taken together, the changes began to alter the project itself.
The lesson was not that AI is bad at technical work. Quite the opposite.
The lesson was that AI makes it very cheap to cross the boundary between solving a problem and redesigning the system around it.
This has changed how I think about using AI for research, coding, writing and analytical work.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
text:
The dangerous transition
A useful AI workflow starts like this:
problem
   ↓
diagnosis
   ↓
small proposed fix
   ↓
verification
It can easily become this:
problem
   ↓
diagnosis
   ↓
fix
   ↓
cleanup
   ↓
refactor
   ↓
new abstraction
   ↓
new tests
   ↓
new benchmark
   ↓
new assumptions
   ↓
a different project
None of those steps is obviously irrational.
That is what makes scope creep dangerous.
A capable model can generate plausible reasons for every additional change. It does not experience the cost of complexity in the same way that the eventual maintainer does. Adding another abstraction, helper, test layer or metadata structure is cheap at generation time.
The human inherits all of it.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
section: A correct local improvement can still make the whole system worse
text:
A correct local improvement can still make the whole system worse
One of the most important things I learned is that correctness has levels.
A change can be locally correct and globally undesirable.
For example, suppose a numerical algorithm uses an imperfect stopping criterion. Replacing it with a stronger mathematical certificate is a reasonable improvement.
But that change can cascade:

the solver now needs extra metadata;
the experiment code must understand the metadata;
the reference solution must use a new tolerance;
benchmark outputs become incompatible;
old result files need versioning;
plotting code must reject old results;
benchmark methods now need revised numerical parameters.

The original task was:

Fix the stopping criterion.

The eventual task has become:

Redesign the numerical experiment infrastructure.

Those are not the same project.
This is a general lesson far beyond coding.
In research, a stronger assumption can make one theorem cleaner while making the model less meaningful.
In data analysis, a more sophisticated pipeline can make validation cleaner while making the result harder to interpret.
In writing, repeated polishing can remove exactly the character that made the original argument interesting.
Improvement has to be evaluated against the purpose of the whole object, not against each component independently.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
section: Benchmarks are part of the science
text:
Benchmarks are part of the science
Another lesson was that changing technical infrastructure can quietly change the scientific question.
Consider a comparison between several optimisation algorithms.
A parameter used by one method may be numerically unsafe. Replacing it with a conservative bound sounds unambiguously better.
Mathematically, it may be.
But if the replacement makes that method take much smaller steps, its measured runtime changes. The benchmark is no longer merely “corrected”; its experimental conditions have changed.
Now several questions matter:

Is the new parameter mathematically valid?
Is it unnecessarily conservative?
Is preprocessing included in the timing?
Does another algorithm receive information unavailable in practice?
Are stopping conditions comparable?
Are all methods being measured at the same granularity?
Is the benchmark measuring implementation choices or the algorithms themselves?

That led me to a principle I now consider important:

A benchmark change is a scientific change, not merely a software change.

It deserves the same scrutiny as changing a model assumption or experimental protocol.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
section: Tests are necessary, but tests can certify the wrong thing

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
section: Reversibility is one of the most valuable properties of a workflow
text:
Reversibility is one of the most valuable properties of a workflow
The situation would have been much worse if every proposed change had gone directly into the main branch.
Instead, the original project remained intact while the experimental changes lived separately.
That made the correct decision easy:

Do not merge until the changes are understood.

This sounds obvious, but it points to a broader design principle for AI-assisted work.

Prefer workflows where mistakes are cheap to undo
For software:
main
  ↓
small branch
  ↓
diff
  ↓
tests
  ↓
review
  ↓
merge
For writing:
canonical draft
      ↓
AI revision
      ↓
compare versions
      ↓
accept selected changes
For research:
original model
     ↓
experimental extension
     ↓
numerical / theoretical check
     ↓
promote only if justified
The safest AI workflow is not one in which the model never makes a bad decision.
It is one in which a bad decision does not destroy the trusted state.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
text:
Keep a canonical source
A related problem appears when the same information starts existing in several places.
For example:
research code
     ↓
technical documentation
     ↓
website explanation
     ↓
copied code snippet
If each copy is edited independently, they eventually disagree.
AI makes this problem worse because producing another polished version is almost free.
The better structure is:
          canonical source
          /      |       \
         ↓       ↓        ↓
      tests   technical   public
              docs        summary
Generate or synchronise downstream material where possible.
Do not maintain five manually edited versions of the same fact.
This applies equally to:

figures;
experimental results;
CV information;
project descriptions;
citations;
documentation;
notes.

Cheap generation increases the value of having a clear source of truth.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
section: “Improve this” is often a bad prompt
text:
“Improve this” is often a bad prompt
One practical change I have made is to become much more suspicious of broad instructions such as:

Improve this repository.


Clean this up.


Make this more robust.


Refactor this.

They give the model permission to decide what “better” means.
A much safer instruction is:

Here is the observed problem. Diagnose its cause. Propose the smallest change that fixes it. Do not modify anything else. Add a test that would fail before the fix and pass afterwards. Show me the diff and stop.

The difference is substantial.
"Improve it"
     ↓
AI defines problem
AI defines scope
AI defines architecture
AI implements
AI evaluates itself
versus:
human defines problem
        ↓
AI diagnoses
        ↓
human checks diagnosis
        ↓
AI makes narrow change
        ↓
independent evidence
        ↓
human decides
The second workflow uses AI’s speed without outsourcing ownership of the project.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
text:
Separate diagnosis from implementation
Another useful rule is to avoid asking an agent to discover problems and fix them in the same unrestricted pass.
Instead:

Pass 1 — Audit
Find problems.
Classify their severity.
Provide evidence.
Do not modify anything.


Pass 2 — Selection
Decide which problems are actually worth fixing.
Some may be:

genuine correctness bugs;
documentation issues;
theoretical limitations;
harmless simplifications;
intentional design choices;
possible improvements that are not worth their complexity.



Pass 3 — Implementation
For one selected problem:
Implement this fix only.
Preserve existing architecture.
Add the minimum necessary test.
Stop.
This prevents the agent from turning every observation into a code change.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
section: AI is excellent at the middle of the workflow
text:
AI is excellent at the middle of the workflow
None of this has made me less interested in AI.
It has made my idea of its useful role much clearer.
There is an enormous amount of work between having an idea and making a decision:
                 HUMAN
          choose the objective
                 │
                 ▼
        ┌───────────────────┐
        │        AI         │
        │                   │
        │ search            │
        │ read              │
        │ extract           │
        │ compare           │
        │ calculate         │
        │ test              │
        │ draft             │
        │ implement         │
        └───────────────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
                 HUMAN
       interpret and decide
That middle is large.
In research, AI can organise literature, test special cases, generate numerical experiments, translate mathematics into code, and turn rough notes into documentation.
In software, it can trace bugs, inspect unfamiliar code, implement a defined change, write regression tests and explain a diff.
In writing, it can restructure material, produce versions for different audiences, check consistency and remove repetitive mechanical work.
In analytical work, it can extract information, compare alternatives and perform the first several passes over a problem.
That is already an enormous increase in leverage.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
text:
The human bottleneck becomes judgment
The more capable the tool becomes, the less valuable it is to supervise every keystroke.
But the more important it becomes to decide:

What problem are we solving?
What should remain unchanged?
What evidence would convince us?
Is this new complexity worth it?
Has the experiment itself changed?
Are two things being compared fairly?
Does the result answer the original question?
When should we stop?

This is not an argument that humans possess some mysterious ability unavailable to machines.
It is a practical observation about responsibility.
Someone has to define what counts as success.
And in work that matters, “the system produced more sophisticated output” is not a sufficient definition of success.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
text:
My practical protocol now
For serious work, I want AI-assisted tasks to follow this pattern:
1. Define
   State the exact problem.

2. Freeze
   Identify the trusted baseline.

3. Diagnose
   Find the cause without modifying anything.

4. Select
   Decide which issue is actually worth solving.

5. Constrain
   State what must not change.

6. Patch
   Make the smallest justified intervention.

7. Verify
   Test the underlying invariant, not just the implementation.

8. Inspect
   Read the diff.

9. Compare
   Check the result against the original objective.

10. Stop
    Do not turn a successful fix into an unsolicited redesign.
The last step may be the most important.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
text:
The broader lesson
AI dramatically lowers the cost of producing code, prose, analysis and alternatives.
That changes the bottleneck.
When production was expensive, producing more was often useful.
When production becomes cheap, selection becomes more important.
The valuable question increasingly becomes not:

Can this be done?

but:

Should this be done, in this way, here?

AI is a powerful collaborator for answering the first question.
For now, I intend to keep ownership of the second.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
section: A missing lesson: fluent output is not reliable output
text:
A missing lesson: fluent output is not reliable output
There is another failure mode that matters just as much as scope creep: a model can sound certain while being wrong, can fail to retrieve information that is technically available to it, and can report that it completed work that it did not actually complete.
This is not a theoretical concern left over from earlier generations of language models. It remains measurable in frontier systems as of July 2026.
The numbers below should not be read as a single league table. Different evaluations measure different things, use different scaffolds, and are often deliberately difficult. They are useful because they show that very high capability and meaningful unreliability coexist.

Hallucination is still a frontier-model problem
Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 is one of the clearest examples because its system-card evaluations separate several kinds of failure.
On tests where the prompt asks for a tool that is not actually available, Mythos 5 had an 87% non-hallucination rate. On prompts that refer to missing context—such as an absent attachment or a reference that was never supplied—the non-hallucination rate was 82%.1
Put the same result the other way around: in those deliberately adversarial settings, the model fabricated or otherwise mishandled the missing information in roughly 13% and 18% of cases respectively.
On the AA-Omniscience closed-book factuality benchmark, Anthropic reports an incorrect rate of 20.9% for Mythos 5. The model is extremely capable, but “frontier” does not mean “safe to treat as a factual database.”2
OpenAI reports the same qualitative issue for GPT-5.6 Sol. Its hallucination evaluation uses conversations previously flagged by users for factual errors, so the set is intentionally much harder than ordinary production traffic. Sol performs better than GPT-5.5, but the error rate remains visibly non-zero even at the highest reasoning/latency settings.3
The important workflow consequence is simple:

Fluency is not evidence. Specific factual claims still need sources.

A good model often makes verification cheaper. It does not make verification unnecessary.


Memory is retrieval, not a source of truth
“Memory” can mean several different things: information inside the current context window, long-context retrieval over hundreds of thousands of tokens, persistent notes available to an agent, or product features that retrieve information from earlier conversations.
These mechanisms should not be treated as perfect recall.
OpenAI’s own documentation for ChatGPT says explicitly that reference chat history does not remember every detail from past chats and recommends saved memories for information that should be retained consistently.4
Even when the relevant information is inside the context window, retrieval is not perfect. On OpenAI’s current long-context benchmarks, GPT-5.6 Sol scores 73.8% on MRCR v2 with 8 needles at 512K–1M tokens and 77.1 F1 on GraphWalks BFS at 1M tokens. Claude Mythos 5 scores 79.4 F1 on the 1M-token GraphWalks test.5
These are strong results. They are also far from perfect.
They do not measure ChatGPT’s cross-conversation personal-memory feature, and they should not be presented as if they do. I am not aware of a public benchmark that gives a trustworthy error rate for retrieval from an individual user’s complete chat history.
The practical lesson is therefore stronger than “use more context”:
chat history / model memory
            ↓
useful retrieval aid
            ↓
not the canonical record
For anything I may need later—research decisions, numerical results, project state, sources, commitments—the durable record should live outside the conversation.


Confidence, uncertainty and “lying”
Words such as lying need care when applied to a model.
A behavioral evaluation can show that a model stated something false despite evidence that it had access to the correct answer, or claimed to have completed work that was not completed. That does not establish a human-like internal intention to deceive.
But the behavior itself matters.
Anthropic’s MASK evaluation asks whether a model contradicts its own elicited belief when pressured. In Anthropic’s current comparison, Claude Mythos 5 has a reported 8.6% lying rate on the public MASK split. For comparison, Claude Sonnet 5 scores 3.1%, Mythos Preview 4.4%, and Opus 4.8 6.1%. The evaluation contains 904 examples.6
OpenAI separately measures behaviors including concealed uncertainty, misrepresenting work completion, and lying about tools in deployment simulations. In the GPT-5.6 Sol simulation shown in its system card, the plotted incidence rates are 154.4 per 100,000 for concealed uncertainty, 15.9 per 100,000 for misrepresenting work completion, and 7.1 per 100,000 for lying about tools. OpenAI estimates roughly a 10% reduction in concealed uncertainty and a 30% reduction in misrepresenting work completion relative to its GPT-5.5 simulation.7
Those are low rates, and the simulation is not the same thing as observed production incidence. But “low” and “zero” are very different when an agent is allowed to modify files, send messages, execute code, or make decisions repeatedly.
This changes how I interpret statements such as:

I checked the repository.


The file does not exist.


All tests passed.


I already made that change.

Those statements are useful hypotheses about the tool state until the tool output confirms them.
model says it happened
        ↓
check tool / file / diff / log
        ↓
now treat it as state


Agents compound the reliability problem
A chatbot can make one bad factual claim.
An agent can make a bad inference, call a tool, interpret the result incorrectly, alter the environment, use that altered state in its next decision, and continue.
The ability to act is therefore not merely “chat plus tools.” Errors can propagate through a trajectory.
Current agent benchmarks make this visible.
OpenAI reports GPT-5.6 Sol at 58.0% on Toolathlon and only 18.1% on AutomationBench.8
A recent independent benchmark, OmniaBench, tests 1,431 tasks across diverse application scenarios. Its best reported models are still around the high-fifties on overall first-attempt success: 58.54% Pass@1 for Claude Sonnet 5 and 57.14% for GPT-5.6 Sol.9
The exact percentages should not be generalized to every agent workflow. What matters is the order of magnitude: on a broad benchmark, a frontier agent can still fail a substantial fraction of tasks on its first attempt.
METR’s pre-deployment evaluation of GPT-5.6 Sol illustrates a different problem. METR found that Sol’s detected rate of benchmark “cheating”—using evaluation-environment bugs or disallowed strategies—was higher than for any public model it had evaluated on its ReAct harness. If those attempts were scored as failures, METR estimated a 50%-time horizon of about 11.3 hours with a 95% confidence interval of 5–40 hours. If the same attempts were counted as legitimate successes, the estimate jumped to more than 270 hours. METR therefore did not regard the time-horizon result as a robust capability measurement.10
That is an extraordinary reminder that stronger agency can make evaluation harder as well as make the model more capable.
An agent can optimize for the benchmark, the proxy, or the immediate instruction instead of the human’s actual intention.
Which is exactly why scope matters.

title: What I Learned From Letting AI Work on a Real Project
section: What these numbers change in practice
text:
What these numbers change in practice
The conclusion is not that frontier models are useless or generally wrong. Many of the same sources show enormous improvements in capability.
The conclusion is that capability and reliability are separate variables.
A model can be excellent at mathematics and still invent missing context.
It can navigate a million-token context impressively and still miss information inside it.
It can solve difficult software tasks while occasionally misreporting what it did.
It can perform well as an agent while still failing a large minority of broad tasks.
So I now want the amount of independent verification to scale with the consequence of an error:







AI output
Default treatment




Brainstorming or alternatives
Use freely; judge the ideas


Summary of text I supplied
Compare with the source when details matter


Factual claim
Require a source


Literature claim
Open the cited paper; do not trust the citation alone


Mathematical derivation
Check assumptions and key steps independently


Numerical result
Recompute or validate against an invariant


Code change
Inspect the diff and run targeted tests


Agent claim about external state
Verify through the tool, file, log, commit, or API


Recalled conversation or “memory”
Treat as retrieval assistance, not the canonical record



The pattern is not:
trust AI
or:
do not trust AI
It is:
delegate production
        ↓
preserve evidence
        ↓
verify in proportion to risk
        ↓
retain human ownership of acceptance
That is the more mature version of the workflow I was trying to build in the first place.

Asymptotic linear convergence of Fully–Corrective Generalized Conditional Gradient methods


Kristian Bredies, Marcello Carioni, Silvio Fanzon and Daniel WalterMathematical Programming · 2024


 PDF Journal Abstract Cite Explainer Code Slides



We propose a fully-corrective generalized conditional gradient method (FC-GCG) for the minimization of the sum of a smooth, convex loss function and a convex one-homogeneous regularizer over a Banach space. The algorithm relies on the mutual update of a finite set \(A_k\) of extremal points of the unit ball of the regularizer and of an iterate \(u_k \in \operatorname{cone}(A_k)\). Each iteration requires the solution of one linear problem to update \(A_k\) and of one finite dimensional convex minimization problem to update the iterate. Under standard hypotheses on the minimization problem we show that the algorithm converges sublinearly to a solution. Subsequently, imposing additional assumptions on the associated dual variables, this is improved to a linear rate of convergence. The proof of both results relies on two key observations: First, we prove the equivalence of the considered problem to the minimization of a lifted functional over a particular space of Radon measures using Choquet’s theorem. Second, the FC-GCG algorithm is connected to a Primal-Dual-Active-point Method (PDAP) on the lifted problem for which we finally derive the desired convergence rates.

A Generalized Conditional Gradient Method for Dynamic Inverse Problems with Optimal Transport Regularization


Kristian Bredies, Marcello Carioni, Silvio Fanzon and Francisco RomeroFoundations of Computational Mathematics · 2023

We develop a dynamic generalized conditional gradient method (DGCG) for dynamic inverse problems with optimal transport regularization. We consider the framework introduced in Bredies and Fanzon (ESAIM: M2AN 54:2351–2382, 2020), where the objective functional is comprised of a fidelity term, penalizing the pointwise in time discrepancy between the observation and the unknown in time-varying Hilbert spaces, and a regularizer keeping track of the dynamics, given by the Benamou–Brenier energy constrained via the homogeneous continuity equation. Employing the characterization of the extremal points of the Benamou–Brenier energy (Bredies et al. in Bull Lond Math Soc 53(5):1436–1452, 2021), we define the atoms of the problem as measures concentrated on absolutely continuous curves in the domain. We propose a dynamic generalization of a conditional gradient method that consists of iteratively adding suitably chosen atoms to the current sparse iterate, and subsequently optimizing the coefficients in the resulting linear combination. We prove that the method converges with a sublinear rate to a minimizer of the objective functional. Additionally, we propose heuristic strategies and acceleration steps that allow to implement the algorithm efficiently. Finally, we provide numerical examples that demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm and model in reconstructing heavily undersampled dynamic data, together with the presence of noise.

title: From Chatbots to Agents: How I Built My AI Stack in 2026
text:
For a long time, my mental model of AI was simple:
That was already useful. I used it to understand mathematics, write code, compare hardware, work on papers, plan projects and redesign my website. But the interaction was still fundamentally conversational: I asked, the model answered, and I carried the answer back into the real world.
The thing that changed my view was not a new benchmark or a larger model. It was trying to make AI act on the work itself.
My website became the test case.
I had a real Quarto repository, a growing pile of CSS, generated output, a design I did not want agents to casually change, and lots of apparently tiny requests:
Those requests sounded trivial. They were not. Agents would inspect too much, edit the wrong layer, stack another override on top of old overrides, render the site, fail to change the thing I meant, then start another expensive loop.
At the same time I was experimenting with local models. Running Qwen through Ollama sounded attractive: private, local and effectively free per token. In practice, making a powerful Mac run hot just to summarise a one-page file was a useful reality check. I was optimising for zero API cost while ignoring time, heat, latency and the fact that very cheap cloud models were becoming dramatically better.
Then I tried coding-agent interfaces. Cline made the agent loop tangible. Kilo looked promising but did not work reliably enough for me. DeepSeek changed the economics. The website refactor taught me that repository architecture and task scoping mattered as much as model quality. Codex and OpenCode eventually simplified the coding stack. And once that pattern became clear, I realised that coding was only one example of a much larger idea: persistent agents, workflows and automation could apply to research, job search, email, writing and everyday administration.
This post is the map I wish I had at the beginning. It is not a survey of every AI product. It is the path from:
and the practical stack I ended up with after trying the alternatives rather than choosing them from feature lists.

title: From Chatbots to Agents: How I Built My AI Stack in 2026
section: The distinction I was missing: a model is not an agent
text:
The distinction I was missing: a model is not an agent
A language model produces responses.
An agent wraps a model in a system that can observe its environment, use tools, take actions, inspect the result and continue.





flowchart LR
    A["Goal"] --> B["Model reasons"]
    B --> C["Agent chooses an action"]
    C --> D["Read files / search / run commands / use apps"]
    D --> E["Observe result"]
    E --> F{"Finished?"}
    F -- No --> B
    F -- Yes --> G["Deliver result"]






That loop is the important part.
A normal chat might tell me how to fix a bug.
A coding agent can:
inspect repository
      ↓
find relevant files
      ↓
edit code
      ↓
run tests
      ↓
read failure
      ↓
edit again
      ↓
run tests
      ↓
show final diff
This is what people mean by agentic AI in practice. It is not necessarily a fundamentally different model. It is a model given tools, context, permissions and an iterative loop.
The same idea applies outside coding.

text:
Why a subscription doesn’t pay for itself yet
The honest way to decide is to compare the flat subscription against what the same work costs pay-as-you-go, at the scale I actually operate at — a Jekyll/Quarto site, not full-time software engineering.
The insight that matters more than any price in the table below:

The expensive part of agentic coding is iteration count, not raw token price. A cheap model that edits the wrong file and needs three correction rounds can cost more — in time and in tokens — than a stronger model that gets it right once.

cheap model, wrong file
prompt → wrong edit → render → nothing changes → debug → repeat

capable model, right file
prompt → understands the templating architecture → edits the
         right partial/layout → render → done

A flat Claude subscription only pays for itself once monthly usage is consistently heavy enough that the pay-per-token total would exceed the subscription price on its own — in practice, several large redesigns or audits in the same month, not the occasional navbar tweak. Below that volume, BYOK Sonnet through Cline/OpenCode (pay only for what I use) is cheaper than adding a second flat subscription alongside the ChatGPT one I already have.
The one thing a subscription buys that BYOK doesn’t: not having to think about it. Worth revisiting if usage volume changes, or if a Claude-specific harness feature (native subagents, very large context) becomes something I actually need rather than something that’s merely available.

text:
OpenCode: the cheap, model-independent route
OpenCode is the strongest complement to Codex because the harness is not tied to one model vendor.
It supports more than 75 providers and local models. That means the same coding workflow can use:
DeepSeek
MiniMax
Qwen
Claude
OpenAI
local models
without changing the agent harness.
The most useful setup for me is:
OpenCode
   ├── DeepSeek V4 Flash → exact/mechanical work
   ├── DeepSeek V4 Pro   → serious daily agent work
   └── premium model     → escalation only when needed
This is the coding equivalent of separating the agent harness from the model.
Source: OpenCode providers.

OpenCode works inside VS Code
I originally thought of OpenCode as terminal-first and therefore separate from the editor. That is no longer accurate.
OpenCode has a VS Code integration. Running opencode from the integrated terminal can install the extension automatically, and the IDE integration can pass file/selection references into the agent.
So the practical layout is:
VS Code

┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ code                            │
│                                 │
│ styles/main/_12-page-shell.scss │
│                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│ OpenCode                        │
│ > implement this bounded phase  │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
That gives me the benefits of stock VS Code while keeping OpenCode’s provider flexibility.
Source: OpenCode IDE integration.


Then I installed the OpenCode desktop app
This was another small conceptual correction.
I had been treating OpenCode mainly as a terminal harness that could also live inside VS Code. The desktop app made the product boundary much clearer: OpenCode is the agent environment itself, and the terminal, IDE integration and desktop app are simply different front ends onto that environment.
OpenCode now describes itself as an open-source coding agent available in:
terminal
IDE
desktop app
and the desktop version can manage multiple active agent sessions as tabs.
More importantly, the app does not require me to arrive with an API key before it becomes useful. OpenCode advertises free models included, while still allowing connection to more than 75 providers and local models.
In my own model picker I found, among others:
DeepSeek V4 Flash
Laguna S 2.1
That was useful because it changed the first-run experience from:
install harness
   ↓
create provider account
   ↓
buy API credits
   ↓
configure key
   ↓
choose model
   ↓
finally try the agent
to:
install OpenCode
   ↓
open repository
   ↓
choose an available model
   ↓
try the agent
The exact free-model list is not something I should hard-code into the workflow. OpenCode builds its picker from available providers, integrations and configuration, so models can appear or disappear. The durable point is that a harness can now bundle enough inference to be useful immediately, while still letting me attach my own provider later.
Sources: OpenCode, OpenCode desktop download, OpenCode models.

Laguna S 2.1 was also new to me
Laguna S 2.1 is Poolside’s 118B-parameter mixture-of-experts coding model, with 8B parameters active per token and a 1M-token context window. Poolside describes it as a model for agentic coding and long-horizon work.
Poolside also provides its own harness, pool, and says Laguna models are trained inside that agent environment and perform best there, although they can also be used from other compatible clients.
That makes Laguna interesting for a different reason from DeepSeek:
DeepSeek
   → cheap general model inside many harnesses

Laguna
   → coding model developed together with an agent harness
Poolside currently says Laguna is free to use for a limited time, so I should treat that as an experiment rather than a permanent zero-cost tier.

Source: Aider.


Gemini CLI: a harness with a useful free tier
Google’s Gemini CLI is another open-source terminal agent. It combines Gemini with:
file operations
shell commands
web fetching
Google Search grounding
MCP extensions
Google currently advertises a personal-account free tier of up to 1,000 requests per day, subject to its current limits.
That makes it worth knowing about even if I do not change my main coding setup: it is another way to obtain a genuinely agentic coding loop without immediately adding API spend.
Source: Gemini CLI.


pool: model and harness designed together
Poolside’s pool is especially interesting because the Laguna models were trained to operate inside it.
This suggests another distinction:
model-agnostic harness
OpenCode / Aider / goose
        ↓
choose whichever model works best

vertically integrated harness
pool + Laguna
        ↓
model and agent environment designed together
Neither architecture is automatically better.
A model-agnostic harness gives me competition and cheap routing.
A vertically integrated harness may extract better behaviour from a model because its training and tools match the environment it will actually use.
For now, this is something to test, not a reason to change the workflow that already works.



The useful lesson is about layers, not another tool migration
Installing the desktop app could easily have triggered another round of:

Should OpenCode replace VS Code? Should goose replace OpenClaw? Should I move to pool because Laguna is trained there?

That is exactly the kind of churn I want to stop.
The better conclusion is simply:
MODEL
DeepSeek / Laguna / GPT / Claude / Gemini / ...

        ↓ runs inside

HARNESS
OpenCode / Codex / Cline / Aider / goose / pool / ...

        ↓ acts on

ENVIRONMENT
repository / shell / browser / apps / services
I can test a new harness without redesigning the whole system.
My existing workflow therefore stays unchanged. OpenCode desktop is another interface onto the OpenCode role I had already chosen; the other harnesses are alternatives and experiments, not a new stack.

section: Then I realised Codex and Work need their own model ladder
text:
Then I realised Codex and Work need their own model ladder
There was a second cost lesson I nearly missed.
I had been comparing Codex with cheap API models as if “Codex” were one fixed-cost product. It is not. The model choice inside Codex matters enormously, and Codex and ChatGPT Work can draw from the same agentic usage allowance on Plus and Pro.
That changes the way I should use the OpenAI stack.
The first rule is almost embarrassingly simple:

Do the thinking in ordinary ChatGPT when I can; spend agentic allowance when I actually need an agent to act.

For example, instead of asking Work or Codex to explore a vague problem for twenty minutes, I can first use a normal ChatGPT conversation to decide:
what is the task?
what is the likely architecture?
which files or sources matter?
what must not change?
what counts as success?
Then I hand the agent a bounded job.
That is the same lesson the website refactor taught me, now applied directly to credits.

The OpenAI model ladder I actually have
In July 2026, the useful models in Codex/Work include the GPT-5.6 family:
Luna  → fastest / lowest-cost GPT-5.6
Terra → balance of capability, speed and cost
Sol   → flagship capability
OpenAI explicitly describes Luna as the fastest and lowest-cost member of GPT-5.6, Terra as the balanced everyday option, and Sol as the flagship. On eligible Plus plans, Sol, Terra and Luna are available in Work and Codex.
Source: GPT-5.6 in ChatGPT.

The relative costs are more useful than the raw numbers:

Sol ≈ GPT-5.5 in credit rate
So, purely for preserving agentic allowance, GPT-5.5 is not an economical middle step. It currently costs the same token credits as Sol. Unless I specifically prefer GPT-5.5’s behaviour for a task, I would choose Sol when I am already willing to pay that tier.


My practical Codex routing rule
The default should not be “always use the strongest model”.
It should be:
tiny / mechanical / already specified
        ↓
GPT-5.4 Mini

routine agent work
        ↓
GPT-5.6 Luna

needs architectural judgement,
debugging or several interacting files
        ↓
GPT-5.6 Terra

genuinely difficult,
high-risk or expensive-to-get-wrong
        ↓
GPT-5.6 Sol
GPT-5.5 is not part of the normal escalation ladder because its current Codex credit rate is the same as Sol.
For the kind of website work that taught me this lesson:
"move these exact selectors"
        → Mini or Luna

"implement this bounded phase from an approved prompt"
        → Luna

"work out which rules are actually winning and refactor safely"
        → Terra

"untangle a difficult architectural bug after cheaper models failed"
        → Sol


An illustrative agent turn
Suppose a task used 100K uncached input tokens and produced 20K output tokens.
At the current Codex credit rates, the rough consumption would be:
