This is only an illustration; real tasks vary substantially in context, cached input, output length and tool loops.
But it shows why the routing decision matters. A routine task on Luna can use roughly one fifth of the credits of the same token mix on Sol.


The other ways to preserve agentic allowance
Model choice is only part of it.
1. Keep routine work out of the shared pool where practical.
Codex and Work share agentic usage. Ordinary ChatGPT is therefore the better place for preliminary thinking, prompt design, explanation and review that does not require the agent to act on files or tools.
2. Give the agent the smallest useful scope.
bad:
"review the repo and improve the CSS"

better:
"edit only these two files; preserve appearance;
run render + quick tests; stop if ownership is ambiguous"
Less wandering means less input, less output and fewer loops.
3. Prefer Luna over Sol as the normal starting point.
Luna is not merely a “cheap emergency model”. It is the cost-efficient member of the current flagship family. Terra is the escalation when the task genuinely needs more judgement.
4. Use Mini for genuinely mechanical work.
Mini is cheaper than Luna on the current rate card. I should use it when the task has already been fully reasoned through and failure is easy to detect.
5. Avoid Fast mode unless latency is worth the extra credits.
OpenAI says Fast mode consumes credits at a higher rate on supported models.
6. Keep outputs short when long prose is not useful.
Output tokens are the expensive side of the rate card. For coding agents, I want:
make the change
run the checks
show the diff
report only what matters
not a long essay after every edit.
7. Exploit stable context rather than making the agent rediscover architecture.
Cached input is charged at one tenth of normal input for the current GPT-5.6 models. Files such as AGENTS.md, SOURCE_MAP.md and a clean canonical architecture therefore help twice: they reduce reasoning mistakes and make repeated context cheaper.
8. Stop cheap agents when they start looping.
Three failed Luna attempts can be worse than one Terra attempt. The correct optimisation target is still:

credits per successful task, not credits per model call.



Work follows the same strategic rule
OpenAI says Codex, ChatGPT Work and other supported agentic features can draw from the same agentic allowance. The public Plus/Pro documentation does not give me a simple fixed “Work task = N credits” table, because consumption depends on the task and model.
So I use the same conservative routing idea:
simple research / file handling
        → Luna

multi-source synthesis / judgement
        → Terra

difficult, long, high-value workflow
        → Sol
And before launching Work, I ask whether the task actually needs Work at all.
If ordinary ChatGPT can produce the plan, comparison or draft without acting across files/tools, I save the agentic pool for the part that genuinely benefits from an agent.
The old toolkit summary had the right principle but was too tied to specific promotional model names and prices.
The durable strategy is:
routine, non-sensitive
        ↓
best current FREE hosted model

need more reliability
        ↓
strong economical cloud model

genuinely hard
        ↓
frontier model / Codex
Specific free endpoints change quickly. Rather than permanently standardising on one Gemini, DeepSeek or other promotional model, I should use the strongest current free option exposed by the interface I am using.

That is why better prompts, cleaner repository architecture and explicit stop conditions matter as much as model price.

title: From Chatbots to Agents: How I Built My AI Stack in 2026
section: The escalation ladder now exists inside a single vendor too
text:
The escalation ladder now exists inside a single vendor too
The FREE → CHEAP/VALUE → FRONTIER ladder above used to mean switching vendors. That is changing: major labs now ship the same underlying model as several named capability tiers, trading reasoning depth against speed and cost within one family.
fastest / cheapest tier   → high-volume, low-stakes, latency-sensitive
balanced tier             → the everyday default for most tasks
flagship tier              → hardest reasoning, slowest, most expensive
The practical implication is the same routing discipline as before, just one level more granular: default to the balanced tier, drop to the fast tier for trivial high-volume work, and reserve the flagship tier for the genuinely hard cases — rather than sending every request to the most capable (and slowest) option out of habit. The specific tier names will change with each model generation; the pattern of “one family, three depths” looks durable.

section: Qwen is not only a local model
text:
Qwen is not only a local model
The local Qwen models described later in this note are one branch of a much larger family. Alibaba also serves Qwen as a hosted API, and the coding/cost-efficient variants are genuinely competitive with Western frontier pricing rather than merely “cheap but worse”:
Qwen hosted API
  │
  ├── small/cheap coding-tuned tier   → near-DeepSeek pricing, coding-focused
  ├── mid tier (dense or MoE)         → strong general + coding balance
  └── reasoning-native flagship       → frontier-adjacent quality at a
                                         fraction of Western frontier cost
The flagship hosted tier is the interesting one: independent benchmarks put it ahead of a GPT-4-class model on agentic coding/terminal tasks at roughly a quarter of the price. That makes it a genuine “capable but still cheap” escalation step — one I’d reach for before a frontier subscription model, not just before nothing.






Note“Free” needs a definition



Several providers advertise free tiers that turn out to be a one-time signup token grant rather than a standing allowance — after the grant, they’re simply cheap, not free. Before I standardise on a provider as “the free option,” I check whether that’s a recurring daily quota or a one-time credit, since the practical routing decision differs.

section: My current local stack: three Qwens
text:
My current local stack: three Qwens
With 48 GB unified memory, I do not need one local model for everything. I keep three clearly separated roles:







Model
Role




Qwen3.5 9B
Trivial sensitive work: small summaries, private forms, simple extraction or rewriting


Qwen3.6 27B
Serious private general work: documents, maths, reasoning, research and analysis


Qwen3.6 27B Coding NVFP4
Local coding and repository work



# Pull the three base models
ollama pull qwen3.5:9b
ollama pull qwen3.6:27b
ollama pull qwen3.6:27b-coding-nvfp4

# Keep the custom Modelfiles together
mkdir -p ~/ollama-modelfiles
cd ~/ollama-modelfiles

# Lightweight general model with a larger working context
cat > Modelfile-qwen9-128k <<'EOF'
FROM qwen3.5:9b
PARAMETER num_ctx 131072
EOF
ollama create qwen9-128k -f Modelfile-qwen9-128k

# Main general + maths model
cat > Modelfile-qwen27-64k <<'EOF'
FROM qwen3.6:27b
PARAMETER num_ctx 65536
EOF
ollama create qwen27-64k -f Modelfile-qwen27-64k

# Coding / repository agent model
cat > Modelfile-qwen27-code-64k <<'EOF'
FROM qwen3.6:27b-coding-nvfp4
PARAMETER num_ctx 65536
EOF
ollama create qwen27-code-64k -f Modelfile-qwen27-code-64k

# Check the custom models
ollama list
The 9B model is not my default for difficult work. Its point is speed and low overhead when the task is simple but the material is sensitive. For anything important, I move straight to one of the 27B models.
I give the 9B model a 128K working context, while keeping both 27B models at 64K. The smaller model can afford the extra context more comfortably, which makes it more useful for long documents, larger repository reads and agent sessions without giving up its main advantage: lower memory and compute overhead. The 27B models stay at 64K to preserve more headroom for their much larger weights, the inference runtime and the rest of the Mac.

Why 27B rather than 35B?
Counter-intuitively, the bigger number does not make the 35B version the obvious upgrade.
Qwen3.6-27B is a dense 27B model, while the 35B variant is a mixture-of-experts model. I therefore keep the 27B models as the serious local tier rather than adding 35B simply because it is larger.
The practical rule is:
tiny + sensitive      → qwen9-128k
maths / general       → qwen27-64k
local coding          → qwen27-code-64k
hardest work          → strong cloud model / Codex

title: From Chatbots to Agents: How I Built My AI Stack in 2026
section: Stronger reasoning; cheaper execution when the task allows it
text:
Stronger reasoning; cheaper execution when the task allows it
For an ambiguous task, the first job is to understand the architecture.
That planning step can happen in:
ChatGPT
Codex
DeepSeek V4 Pro
GPT-5.4 mini / frontier model
It should answer:

what is the canonical source?
which files actually participate?
what currently wins in the cascade or build pipeline?
what must remain unchanged?
what is the smallest safe implementation phase?

Once that is known, a cheaper worker can execute an exact prompt:
reasoning / architecture
        ↓
ChatGPT / Codex / V4 Pro

approved bounded implementation
        ↓
OpenCode + V4 Flash
For a difficult coding task, there is no requirement to split planning and acting between tools. Codex can own the whole implementation loop. The split matters when the task is already understood and I want to minimise routine agent cost.

title: From Chatbots to Agents: How I Built My AI Stack in 2026
section: Small phases beat one giant autonomous task
text:
Small phases beat one giant autonomous task
The website cleanup made this concrete.
Instead of:
"clean up the CSS architecture"
the useful sequence was closer to:
Phase 1
audit only
no edits

Phase 2A
consolidate navbar into one canonical stylesheet

Phase 2A.1
move two shared chrome variables into the token file

Phase 2B
consolidate footer into one canonical stylesheet
Each task had:

an explicit objective;
an allow-list of files;
explicit files that must not change;
values that must remain identical;
cheap validation commands;
stop conditions when the agent discovers unexpected architecture;
a concise required final report.

This is much cheaper and safer than letting an agent discover the entire repository and refactor it in one run.

title: From Chatbots to Agents: How I Built My AI Stack in 2026
section: The prompt should constrain the search space
text:
The prompt should constrain the search space
A good implementation prompt is not merely detailed prose.
It defines the operating boundary:
allowed files
files that may be created
generated files that must never be edited
values that must remain unchanged
commands to run
tests to run
conditions that mean STOP
definition of done
For example:
DO:
  _00-tokens.scss
  _02-editorial.scss

DO NOT:
  _10-navbar.scss
  docs/
  site_libs/

VERIFY:
  rg ...
  quarto render
  npm run test:quick

STOP IF:
  another source defines the same token differently
This reduces both risk and token burn because the agent does not need to repeatedly rediscover the whole codebase.

title: From Chatbots to Agents: How I Built My AI Stack in 2026
section: Never let generated output become the implementation
text:
Never let generated output become the implementation
A rendered Quarto site can produce many changed files under docs/ and hashed Bootstrap assets even when the source change is tiny.
The rule is:

Source files explain the implementation; generated files only prove the render happened.

For this project, visual changes must originate in canonical source such as:
styles/
_quarto.yml
data/
filters/
content
not in:
docs/
site_libs/
A render may legitimately change generated output, but an agent must never “fix” the site by editing those files directly.

title: From Chatbots to Agents: How I Built My AI Stack in 2026
section: Diff-first review is better than re-reading the whole repository
text:
Diff-first review is better than re-reading the whole repository
Once the architecture is understood, the best review input is usually the Git diff, not another ZIP of the whole directory.
agent changes source
      ↓
local render/tests
      ↓
commit + push
      ↓
review commit diff
The diff tells me:

exactly what source changed;
whether the agent touched unrelated files;
whether a “move” really preserved values;
whether generated output is the only extra noise;
whether the task stayed inside scope.

I only need the full directory again when:

architecture is unclear;
the diff depends on surrounding code not visible in the changed files;
I am doing a new repo-wide audit;
the agent reports an unexpected cross-file dependency.

This gives a useful division:
architecture question
      → inspect repository

implementation review
      → inspect diff first

title: From Chatbots to Agents: How I Built My AI Stack in 2026
section: Commit source refactors separately from render output when useful
text:
Commit source refactors separately from render output when useful
Quarto renders can create a large generated diff. When practical, keeping source refactors easy to identify makes review much easier.
At minimum, I should be able to distinguish:
source commit

Stop cheap models before they loop

It is:

Escalate when the cheaper model stops making reliable progress.

Typical warning signs:
re-reading the same files
adding another override rather than fixing ownership
editing generated output
broadening scope without permission
trying several speculative fixes
re-running expensive validation without a new hypothesis
At that point, moving from Flash to Pro — or from Pro to a premium model — can be cheaper than another five agent iterations.

n8n: use it when the process becomes known
OpenClaw and n8n overlap, but the decision rule is useful:

Uncertain task → agent. Known process → workflow.

OpenClaw is shaped like:
"Find relevant opportunities and decide which matter."
The agent chooses how to reason through the task.
n8n is shaped like:
07:30 trigger
    ↓
fetch sources
    ↓
deduplicate
    ↓
extract fields
    ↓
call model
    ↓
score
    ↓
write database row
    ↓
notify if threshold passed
The workflow itself defines the control flow.
n8n combines explicit workflow logic, integrations, code, AI agents and human approval steps. It is therefore a better place for a process once I know exactly what should happen every time.
Source: n8n AI agents.

OpenClaw and n8n can work together
A mature system can split judgement from plumbing:
                  OpenClaw
                 judgement
                    ▲
                    │
sources ──► n8n ──► model
            │
            │ structured data
            ▼
          tracker
            │
            ▼
         OpenClaw
       prioritisation
            │
            ▼
           me
OpenClaw does not need to perform every deterministic transformation itself. n8n does not need to contain all the judgement.

A job-search agent: the best first OpenClaw project
The job-search workflow is a good first persistent-agent project because it naturally progresses from manual reasoning to useful automation.

Phase 1 — one URL, manually

      ↓

role / salary / location / skills / requirements
      ↓

      ↓

This can be ChatGPT Work or an interactive OpenClaw task.


Phase 2 — let the agent search
selected job sources
      ↓
OpenClaw
      ↓
new relevant adverts
The agent now removes the manual discovery step.


Phase 3 — persistent profile comparison
The agent applies the same standing profile and criteria every time:
new role
   ↓
compare with CV/profile
   ↓
fit score
   ↓
which experiences to emphasise
   ↓
what is missing


Phase 4 — recurring execution
every morning
      ↓
search
      ↓
analyse
      ↓
notify only when worth attention
This is where OpenClaw’s persistence and scheduling become valuable.


Phase 5 — structured tracker
Once the fields are stable, move the repetitive data plumbing into a structured workflow:
advert
  ↓
deduplicate
  ↓
normalise fields
  ↓
score
  ↓
tracker / database
This is a natural point to introduce n8n.


Phase 6 — application material after approval
Only after I decide to pursue the role:
approved role
     ↓
choose relevant experiences
     ↓
tailored CV variant
     ↓
cover-letter / application material
The system should never turn into an uncontrolled application bot. The useful automation is discovery, structuring and prioritisation, with a human decision before outbound application material or submission.
The durable lesson is:

Start with one useful manual agent task, make it persistent with OpenClaw, and only convert the stable repeated parts into n8n workflows later.

section: Knowledge management: chats are scratchpads, Markdown is memory
text:
Knowledge management: chats are scratchpads, Markdown is memory
AI creates a new failure mode: hundreds of useful conversations that cannot be found when I need them.
The solution is to stop treating chats as the archive.

Chats are temporary workspaces. Local Markdown files are the durable source of truth.

I would keep one plain-Markdown knowledge folder, optionally opened as an Obsidian vault and backed by Git:
AI-Notes/
├── INDEX.md
├── INBOX.md
│
├── projects/
│   ├── website/
│   │   ├── README.md
│   │   ├── DECISIONS.md
│   │   └── NEXT.md
│   └── other-project/
│
├── areas/
│   ├── career.md
│   ├── research.md
│   ├── teaching.md
│   └── admin.md
│
├── reference/
│   ├── ai-tools.md
│   ├── coding-workflow.md
│   └── topic-notes/
│
└── archive/

What each file does
INDEX.md — map of the important notes; not a giant document.
INBOX.md — temporary ideas and things to process.
Project README.md — current state, purpose and links.
DECISIONS.md — decisions already made and why, so I do not repeatedly revisit them.
NEXT.md — immediate next actions, not a complete project history.
areas/ — ongoing responsibilities such as career, research or administration.
reference/ — stable knowledge worth reusing.


The rule after a useful AI conversation
Do not save the transcript.
Instead ask:
Did this conversation create...
├── a decision?       → update DECISIONS.md
├── a next action?    → update NEXT.md
├── reusable knowledge? → update reference note
├── project context?  → update project README
└── nothing durable?  → leave it in chat
This keeps the knowledge base small.


Periodic compression





flowchart TD
    C["Chats / papers / experiments"] --> S["Synthesis"]
    S --> P["Project notes"]
    S --> D["Decisions"]
    S --> R["Reference"]
    S --> N["Next actions"]
    P --> A["Archive old material"]






The goal is progressive compression: many chats become a handful of useful notes; old notes become a concise current state.
Plain Markdown is deliberately boring: it is searchable, portable, Git-friendly, readable by every coding agent and unlikely to become obsolete.

text:
How I think about cost now
My priority is predictable cost and using premium capacity only when it materially changes the outcome.
The current value ladder is:
1. Existing ChatGPT subscription
        ↓
2. DeepSeek V4 Flash for scoped routine agent work
        ↓
3. DeepSeek V4 Pro for serious daily agent reasoning
        ↓
4. MiniMax M3 / GPT-5.4 mini when a capability gap appears
        ↓
5. Codex / Sonnet / frontier model for genuinely hard or high-risk work
        ↓
6. Local model for privacy, not routine cost saving
This is a change from the earlier “free first” strategy.
With V4 Flash at $0.14/M uncached input and $0.28/M output, the difference between “free” and “extremely cheap” is often smaller than the cost of a failed agent loop. I should optimise for successful completion per pound, not for zero API spend.
The most interesting paid default is therefore V4 Pro: it is only about 3.1× Flash on normal input/output pricing while remaining inexpensive enough for routine serious work.
I would not add a Claude subscription, Cursor subscription or a large model pool pre-emptively. I can escalate through APIs only when a real task demonstrates that the cheaper layer is insufficient.

The practical division is:

What changed most was not the model I use. It was the unit of work I expect AI to handle.
I started with prompts. I ended up designing systems around repositories, tools, verification, persistent context and explicit handoffs between human judgement and machine execution.
That is the shift I mean when I say I moved from chatbots to agents.
Models, prices and product names will continue to change. That architecture should not need to.

title: How I use AI in technical work
text:
AI is now part of my technical workflow.
I use it to search, compare, draft, test, review and implement faster. In research, it can shorten the distance between a question and a useful map of the literature. In scientific software, it can explain unfamiliar code, trace a bug, propose a regression test or implement a narrowly specified change. In technical communication, it can help turn the same underlying work into a paper, a reproducible repository, a technical walkthrough or an accessible project page.
That is substantial leverage.
It is also easy to misuse.
A model can produce convincing work very quickly, including work that is unnecessary, poorly scoped or simply wrong. An agent can go further: it can act on a mistaken inference, alter the environment, and then continue reasoning from the state it has created.
So I do not think the useful distinction is between using AI and not using AI. The more important distinction is between delegating production and delegating judgment.
My aim is to do the first aggressively and the second cautiously.

title: How I use AI in technical work
section: From a difficult question to a defensible result
text:
From a difficult question to a defensible result
The broader way I work predates current AI tools.
I tend to start with an open-ended problem and try to make it precise: identify the assumptions, decide what is observable, formulate a model, implement it, test what the evidence supports, and communicate the result clearly.
In compact form:
frame the problem
        ↓
model and explore
        ↓
build and test
        ↓
evaluate the evidence
        ↓
communicate the result
AI fits naturally into this process, but it does not replace the process.
A useful division of labour is:
                 HUMAN
          define the problem
                 │
                 ▼
        ┌───────────────────┐
        │        AI         │
        │                   │
        │ search            │
        │ read              │
        │ compare           │
        │ calculate         │
        │ draft             │
        │ test              │
        │ review            │
        │ implement         │
        └───────────────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
                 HUMAN
       verify and decide
The boundary is deliberately porous. AI can suggest a better question, challenge an assumption or notice something I missed. I can also ask it to criticise my conclusions.
What does not move is responsibility for deciding what the project is trying to establish and whether the evidence actually establishes it.

title: How I use AI in technical work
How I use AI in technical work
text:
What I retain
Some decisions sit too close to the substance of the problem to be treated as implementation details.
I retain responsibility for:
Problem formulation. What question are we actually answering? What assumptions are legitimate? What would count as a useful result?
Mathematical reasoning. Definitions, derivations, hypotheses, theoretical claims and the distinction between a plausible argument and a proof.
Experimental design. What is being measured? Are methods being compared fairly? Has a software change silently changed the scientific experiment?
Source selection. Which document, dataset, paper or repository is authoritative?
Interpretation. What does the result establish, what remains uncertain, and which conclusions go beyond the evidence?
Scope. Is a proposed improvement worth the additional complexity?
Acceptance. Does an AI-generated output actually become part of the project?
This is less about protecting tasks from automation than about keeping the chain of reasoning visible.

title: How I use AI in technical work
text:
Research: accelerate exploration, preserve evidence
Research is one of the strongest uses I have found for AI.
At the beginning of a topic, a model can help build an initial map:
question
   ↓
literature reconnaissance
   ↓
methods and assumptions
   ↓
agreements and disagreements
   ↓
promising directions
That is particularly useful when moving into an adjacent area. It can identify terminology, suggest relevant papers, compare formulations and expose assumptions that deserve attention.
For mathematical work, I also use AI as an interactive second reader. Useful questions include:

What happens in the simplest non-trivial case?
Which assumption is doing the real work?
Is there an obvious counterexample if this hypothesis is removed?
Can this statement be reformulated geometrically?
What numerical experiment would distinguish these two explanations?
Which result in the literature is closest to this argument?
Where might this proof fail?

The important distinction is between discovery and evidence.
A model telling me that a paper proves something is not evidence that the paper proves it. A plausible derivation is not a theorem. A numerical value appearing in a conversation is not a reproducible result.
AI can make the route to verification much shorter. It does not eliminate the final verification step.

title: How I use AI in technical work
section: Scientific software: narrow changes beat autonomous improvement
text:
Scientific software: narrow changes beat autonomous improvement
Coding makes the strengths and weaknesses of AI especially visible.
A model can understand a small research repository surprisingly quickly. It can follow execution paths, explain numerical routines, generate test cases and implement changes across several files.
That makes broad prompts tempting:

Improve this repository.


Make this code more robust.


Refactor this implementation.

I increasingly avoid them for established work.
Those prompts allow the model to define both the problem and the meaning of better. A small correction can then expand into a new API, new metadata, new configuration, new benchmark rules and new infrastructure. Every addition may be individually defensible while the project as a whole becomes less transparent.
For technical repositories I prefer:
trusted baseline
      ↓
specific observed problem
      ↓
diagnosis
      ↓
small proposed change
      ↓
targeted test
      ↓
inspect the diff
      ↓
stop
The word stop matters.
AI already makes adding code cheap. The workflow needs to make unnecessary complexity expensive again.

title: How I use AI in technical work
text:
Separate audit from implementation
A particularly useful discipline is to separate finding problems from fixing them.

1. Audit
Ask the model to inspect the project, classify issues and provide evidence.
Do not change anything.


2. Select
Decide which findings are:

genuine correctness problems;
reproducibility problems;
documentation problems;
intentional simplifications;
theoretical limitations;
optional improvements that are not worth their complexity.



3. Implement
Choose one issue and make the smallest justified intervention.
This prevents an audit from becoming an automatic mandate to rewrite every imperfect part of a project.
It also produces a cleaner review trail: diagnosis, decision, patch.

title: How I use AI in technical work
section: Tests should protect ideas, not just code

title: How I use AI in technical work
section: Benchmarks are part of the scientific argument
text:
Benchmarks are part of the scientific argument
Software changes can alter scientific conclusions without changing the underlying model.
Suppose one optimisation method requires a step-size estimate. Replacing an unsafe estimate with a conservative bound may be mathematically valid, but if the new bound is unnecessarily large, the method takes unnecessarily small steps.
The code is now safer.
The benchmark may now be less fair.
Similarly, a timing comparison can change depending on whether preprocessing is included, whether one method receives information derived from the optimum, how frequently objectives are evaluated, or whether stopping criteria represent genuinely comparable accuracy.
That is why I treat benchmark design as part of the scientific work rather than as implementation plumbing.
A benchmark change deserves the same question as a modelling change:

What exactly are we comparing now?

title: How I use AI in technical work
section: Agents: capability changes the failure mode
text:
Agents: capability changes the failure mode
An agent is more than a chatbot with a terminal.
It can inspect files, call tools, edit code, run tests and respond to the results. That can remove a remarkable amount of mechanical work.
It also allows mistakes to propagate.
wrong inference
      ↓
tool action
      ↓
changed environment
      ↓
next inference uses changed state
      ↓
further action
For that reason, I prefer agents with explicit boundaries:

a trusted starting state;
a specific objective;
a clear list of files or systems they may change;
explicit things they must not change;
tests or other evidence for success;
a diff or audit trail before acceptance.

This is not because current agents are incapable. It is because capability and reliability are different properties.

Frontier models are still imperfect agents
Current benchmarks make that distinction concrete.
As of July 2026, OpenAI reports 58.0% on Toolathlon and 18.1% on AutomationBench for GPT-5.6 Sol. On the same Toolathlon table, Claude Mythos 5 scores 61.7%.1
An independent general-agent benchmark, OmniaBench, reports Overall Pass@1 of 58.54% for Claude Sonnet 5 and 57.14% for GPT-5.6 Sol across 1,431 tasks.2
These benchmarks test different environments and should not be compared as if they were one common error rate. They are also not estimates of failure frequency in ordinary day-to-day use.
Their importance is more basic: even frontier systems that are extremely capable can still fail a substantial fraction of demanding agentic tasks.
The right response is not to avoid agents. It is to design workflows in which failure is visible and reversible.

title: How I use AI in technical work
section: Memory and long context are retrieval aids, not canonical records
text:
Memory and long context are retrieval aids, not canonical records
Another easy mistake is to confuse available somewhere with reliably retrievable.
A long conversation, large context window or persistent memory system can contain the information needed to answer a question and still fail to surface the right detail.
Again, current benchmark results illustrate the point. OpenAI reports GPT-5.6 Sol at 73.8% on its MRCR v2 eight-needle test at 512K–1M tokens and 77.1 F1 on the one-million-token GraphWalks BFS evaluation; Claude Mythos 5 scores 79.4 F1 on the latter.3
Those are strong long-context results. They are not perfect recall.
They also do not measure a product’s cross-conversation personal-memory feature, and I would not treat them as if they did.
For my own work, the practical conclusion is:
chat history / model memory
            ↓
useful retrieval layer
            ↓
not the source of truth
Important decisions, results, references and project state belong in durable artefacts: repositories, Markdown notes, Quarto documents, data files and documentation.
AI can help maintain and interrogate that record.
It should not be the record.

title: How I use AI in technical work
text:
Fluent output is not evidence
Modern models are unusually persuasive because uncertainty is not always visible in the prose.
A claim can be specific, well written and wrong.
A citation can look plausible and not support the sentence attached to it.
An agent can say a file was changed, a test passed or a search found nothing.
For consequential work, I try to attach claims to the thing that can actually establish them:







Claim
Evidence I want




A paper says X
The paper


A factual statement is current
A current primary or authoritative source


A derivation is correct
Assumptions and an independent mathematical check


A numerical result holds
Reproducible computation or an invariant


A code change works
Diff + targeted tests


An agent changed something
File, commit, API response or tool output


A previous decision was made
Durable project notes or source history



The required level of verification scales with the consequence of being wrong.
Brainstorming should remain cheap.
Published claims, mathematical conclusions and repository changes should not.

title: How I use AI in technical work
text:
Reversibility is a feature
The safest AI workflow is not one in which the model never makes a poor decision.
It is one in which a poor decision is cheap to undo.
For software:
main
  ↓
small branch
  ↓
diff
  ↓
test
  ↓
review
  ↓
merge
For writing:
canonical text
      ↓
AI revision
      ↓
compare
      ↓
accept selected changes
For research:
established model
      ↓
experimental extension
      ↓
theoretical / numerical check
      ↓
promote only if justified
This is one reason version control matters even more when generation becomes cheap.

title: How I use AI in technical work
text:
Keep one source of truth
AI makes it almost frictionless to produce another version of something.
A project can quickly acquire:
paper
  ↓
repository
  ↓
technical walkthrough
  ↓
project page
  ↓
presentation
  ↓
CV summary
Those are useful layers for different audiences.
They become a liability when each begins to contain its own version of the facts.
I therefore try to make one source authoritative for each type of information and derive or verify downstream representations against it.
A repository can own implementation and version history. A paper can own a published result. Structured project data can own canonical links. A technical walkthrough can explain the implementation without becoming a second implementation.
AI is particularly useful for transforming one authoritative source for another audience.
That is very different from letting it invent five loosely related versions.

title: How I use AI in technical work
section: Technical communication: transformation is a high-value use
text:
Technical communication: transformation is a high-value use
One of my favourite uses of AI is changing the level of explanation without changing the underlying substance.
The same work may need to serve several readers:
research paper
      ↓
technical repository
      ↓
technical walkthrough
      ↓
industry-facing explanation
      ↓
short professional summary
AI can help identify which details each audience needs, remove unnecessary notation, generate an outline, or compare the public explanation against the technical source for drift.
This is a good form of delegation because the transformation can be checked against something authoritative.
The goal is not to make difficult work sound simple.
It is to make the right part of the difficulty visible to the right reader.

title: How I use AI in technical work
text:
AI-assisted does not mean AI-generated
I do not think every project needs an AI badge.
In some projects AI has played a meaningful role: repository audit, test generation, code review, documentation checks, literature reconnaissance or communication across several technical layers.
Those contributions are worth describing when they illuminate the workflow.
In other cases AI may have been no more important than the editor, version-control system or plotting library.
There is no value in labelling everything.
The interesting question is:

What did AI make possible, faster or easier—and what evidence was used to decide that its output was good enough?

That is the distinction I want project pages to make when AI is genuinely part of the story.

title: How I use AI in technical work
text:
My working protocol
For consequential AI-assisted work, I now use a simple sequence.
1. Define
   State the actual problem.

2. Freeze
   Identify the trusted baseline.

3. Diagnose
   Understand the issue before changing it.

4. Select
   Decide which problem is actually worth solving.

5. Constrain
   State what must remain unchanged.

6. Delegate
   Use AI for the expensive middle.

7. Verify
   Test the relevant property independently.

8. Inspect
   Look at the output, source, diff or evidence.

9. Accept
   Decide whether the result belongs in the project.

10. Stop
    Do not turn a completed task into an unsolicited redesign.
The protocol is intentionally conservative.
AI already supplies the speed.
The workflow needs to supply the control.

In this talk we introduce a Frank-Wolfe-type algorithm for sparse optimization in Banach spaces. We propose and analyze a simple variational model for dislocations at semi-coherent interfaces. The energy functional describes the competition between two terms: a surface energy induced by dislocations and a bulk elastic energy, spent to decrease the amount of dislocations needed to compensate the lattice misfit. section: From bookmaker odds to win probabilities
text:
From bookmaker odds to win probabilities
For fractional odds \(a/b\), the raw implied probability is
\[p_{\mathrm{raw}}=\frac{b}{a+b}.\]
The raw probabilities include the bookmaker’s overround, so they are divided by their sum [3]. The Qatar odds are stored as data rather than hard-coded inside an objective function.
odds_to_probs <- function(odds) {
  fractional <- parse_fractional_odds(odds)
  raw <- 1 / (fractional + 1)
  raw / sum(raw)
}

odds <- read_qatar_odds("data/qatar2023_odds.csv")
The recomputed probabilities agree with the values printed in Table 1 up to the rounding of the published table.

title: Who’s actually the best F1 driver?
text:
Exponential race-time calibration
Assume independent finishing times
\[T_i\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i).\]
Then
\[
\Pr(\text{car }i\text{ wins})=
\frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_j\lambda_j}.
\]
The paper proposes minimising
\[
\operatorname{RSS}(\lambda)=
\sum_i\left(\frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_j\lambda_j}-p_i\right)^2.
\]

The scale is not identifiable
The objective only uses normalised rates. Therefore, for every \(c>0\),
\[\lambda_i=c\,p_i\]
has zero RSS. The absolute scale of Table 1 is not estimated by the win probabilities; only the ratios are identified.
The corrected code makes the exact solution the primary implementation:
lambda_from_probs <- function(probs, scale = 1) {
  assert_probabilities(probs)
  scale * probs
}
It also retains a numerical check, but removes the degeneracy by normalising inside the objective and enforces positivity through log-rates:
numerical <- estimate_lambda_numerically(
  odds$implied_probability,
  restarts = 20,
  seed = 1
)
The unit-sum numerical rates agree with lambda = p. To compare with Table 1, the code estimates the common multiplier that best maps the rounded published probabilities to the rounded published lambda column.

title: Who’s actually the best F1 driver?
text:
Time-rank duality and Table 2
The rank model approximates final rank by
\[r_i\sim N(\mu_i,\sigma^2).\]
Using the continuity-corrected event \(r_i\le 1.5\),
\[p_i=\Phi\left(\frac{1.5-\mu_i}{\sigma}\right),\]
so
\[\mu_i=1.5-\sigma\Phi^{-1}(p_i).\]
Because ranks sum to \(n(n+1)/2\), the common standard deviation is
\[
\sigma=
\frac{n-n^2/2}{\sum_i\Phi^{-1}(p_i)}.
\]
implied_rank_params <- function(probs) {
  n <- length(probs)
  z <- qnorm(probs)
  sigma <- (n - n^2 / 2) / sum(z)
  mu <- 1.5 - sigma * z
  list(mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
}

mu_hat(Max Verstappen) = -0.242969
mu_hat(Fernando Alonso) = 10.501519
matching Table 2.

ImportantWhy the previous dual-page version produced a contradiction

We develop a Markov model of curling matches, parametrised by the probability of winning an end and the probability distribution of scoring ends. Asymptotic linear convergence of Fully–Corrective Generalized Conditional Gradient methods


Kristian Bredies, Marcello Carioni, Silvio Fanzon and Daniel WalterMathematical Programming · 2024


 PDF Journal Abstract Cite Explainer Code Slides



We propose a fully-corrective generalized conditional gradient method (FC-GCG) for the minimization of the sum of a smooth, convex loss function and a convex one-homogeneous regularizer over a Banach space. The algorithm relies on the mutual update of a finite set \(A_k\) of extremal points of the unit ball of the regularizer and of an iterate \(u_k \in \operatorname{cone}(A_k)\). Each iteration requires the solution of one linear problem to update \(A_k\) and of one finite dimensional convex minimization problem to update the iterate. Under standard hypotheses on the minimization problem we show that the algorithm converges sublinearly to a solution. Subsequently, imposing additional assumptions on the associated dual variables, this is improved to a linear rate of convergence. The proof of both results relies on two key observations: First, we prove the equivalence of the considered problem to the minimization of a lifted functional over a particular space of Radon measures using Choquet’s theorem. Second, the FC-GCG algorithm is connected to a Primal-Dual-Active-point Method (PDAP) on the lifted problem for which we finally derive the desired convergence rates.

A Generalized Conditional Gradient Method for Dynamic Inverse Problems with Optimal Transport Regularization


Kristian Bredies, Marcello Carioni, Silvio Fanzon and Francisco RomeroFoundations of Computational Mathematics · 2023


 PDF Journal Abstract Cite Code Poster Video



We develop a dynamic generalized conditional gradient method (DGCG) for dynamic inverse problems with optimal transport regularization. We consider the framework introduced in Bredies and Fanzon (ESAIM: M2AN 54:2351–2382, 2020), where the objective functional is comprised of a fidelity term, penalizing the pointwise in time discrepancy between the observation and the unknown in time-varying Hilbert spaces, and a regularizer keeping track of the dynamics, given by the Benamou–Brenier energy constrained via the homogeneous continuity equation. Employing the characterization of the extremal points of the Benamou–Brenier energy (Bredies et al. in Bull Lond Math Soc 53(5):1436–1452, 2021), we define the atoms of the problem as measures concentrated on absolutely continuous curves in the domain. We propose a dynamic generalization of a conditional gradient method that consists of iteratively adding suitably chosen atoms to the current sparse iterate, and subsequently optimizing the coefficients in the resulting linear combination. We prove that the method converges with a sublinear rate to a minimizer of the objective functional. Additionally, we propose heuristic strategies and acceleration steps that allow to implement the algorithm efficiently. Finally, we provide numerical examples that demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm and model in reconstructing heavily undersampled dynamic data, together with the presence of noise.

We study measure-valued solutions of the inhomogeneous continuity equation \(\partial_t \rho_t + \operatorname{div}(v\rho_t) = g\rho_t\), where the coefficients \(v\) and \(g\) are of low regularity. A new superposition principle is proven for positive measure solutions and coefficients for which the recently introduced dynamic Hellinger–Kantorovich energy is finite. This principle gives a decomposition of the solution into curves \(t \mapsto h(t)\delta_{\gamma(t)}\) that satisfy the characteristic system \(\gamma'(t)=v(t,\gamma(t))\), \(h'(t)=g(t,\gamma(t))h(t)\) in an appropriate sense. In particular, it provides a generalization of existing superposition principles to the low-regularity case of \(g\) where characteristics are not unique with respect to \(h\). Two applications of this principle are presented. First, uniqueness of minimal total-variation solutions for the inhomogeneous continuity equation is obtained if characteristics are unique up to their possible vanishing time. Second, the extremal points of dynamic Hellinger–Kantorovich-type regularizers are characterized. Such regularizers arise, for example, in the context of dynamic inverse problems and dynamic optimal transport.

We study the higher gradient integrability of distributional solutions \(u\) to the equation \(\operatorname{div}(\sigma \nabla u)=0\) in dimension two, in the case when the essential range of \(\sigma\) consists of only two elliptic matrices, i.e., \(\sigma \in \{\sigma_1,\sigma_2\}\) a.e. in \(\Omega\). In Nesi et al. (Ann Inst H Poincaré Anal Non Linéaire 31(3):615–638, 2014), for every pair of elliptic matrices \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\), exponents \(p=p_{\sigma_1,\sigma_2}\in(0,+\infty)\) and \(q=q_{\sigma_1,\sigma_2}\in(1,2)\) have been found so that if \(u\in W^{1,q}(\Omega)\) is a solution to the elliptic equation then \(\nabla u\in L^p(\Omega,\mathrm{weak})\), and the optimality of the upper exponent \(p\) has been proved. In this paper we complement the above result by proving the optimality of the lower exponent \(q\). Precisely, we show that for every arbitrarily small \(\delta\), one can find a particular microgeometry, i.e., an arrangement of the sets \(\sigma^{-1}(\sigma_1)\) and \(\sigma^{-1}(\sigma_2)\), for which there exists a solution \(u\) to the corresponding elliptic equation such that \(\nabla u\in L^{q-\delta}\) but \(\nabla u\notin L^q\). The existence of such optimal microgeometries is achieved by convex integration methods, adapting to the present setting the geometric constructions provided in Astala et al. (Ann Scuola Norm Sup Pisa Cl Sci 5(7):1–50, 2008) for the isotropic case.

A Variational Model for Dislocations at Semi-coherent Interfaces


Silvio Fanzon, Mariapia Palombaro and Marcello PonsiglioneJournal of Nonlinear Science · 2017


 PDF Journal Abstract Cite Slides Poster



We propose and analyze a simple variational model for dislocations at semi-coherent interfaces. The energy functional describes the competition between two terms: a surface energy induced by dislocations and a bulk elastic energy, spent to decrease the amount of dislocations needed to compensate the lattice misfit. We prove that, for minimizers, the former scales like the surface area of the interface, the latter like its diameter. The proposed continuum model is built on some explicit computations done in the framework of the semi-discrete theory of dislocations. Even if we deal with finite elasticity, linearized elasticity naturally emerges in our analysis since the far-field strain vanishes as the interface size increases.

In this study we present an approach that combines sub-sampled encoding reconstruction and simultaneous object motion computation. For that purpose Optimal Transport is used as convex regularization for motion-afflicted measurements. It reconstructs explicit pixel-wise motion fields simultaneously to the image series. Results based on simulated data show that 8-frame image series can be reconstructed in great detail from 4-fold undersampled k-space series data from a single coil. A Complex Analysis approach to the isoperimetric inequality


University of Hull, UK


2023/24


AbsURL



Mathematicians consider the isoperimetric inequality a fundamental principle which states that among simple closed curves of a given length, circle has the largest possible area. This work proves the isoperimetric inequality through the application of complex analysis, specifically the Riemann mapping theorem. Each idea is inspired by Peter L. Duren’s monograph, Univalent Functions and Robert Osserman’s paper. The thesis covers a brief history of the inequality and presents a survey of classic proofs of the inequality while giving a constructive proof based on Riemann mapping theorem from the complex analysis. Practical applications will also be explored.

This dissertation inquires into the Euler-Lagrange equation and the method of Lagrange multipliers, with special emphasis on how they apply to variational problems. In particular we are illustrating through some example problems such as the brachistochrone problem that both of these mathematical tools are necessary when seeking an optimal solution for particular field tasks. A marriage of the Euler-Lagrange equation with Lagrange multipliers can turn an obejctive into manageable problems and remove all of their complications. The dissertation tests and verifies the cycloid as the curve of quickest descent in practice, thus confirming the practical usefulness of these methods. More broadly, the dissertation highlights the wide-ranging application and importance of these tools for tackling complex optimization problems.

The Isoperimetric Problem


University of Hull, UK


2022/23


AbsURL



A closed curve’s perimeter and the area it encloses are related by the isoperimetric inequality. It claims that a circle is the closed curve with the biggest area enclosed for all closed curves with a specified perimeter. A circle with the same perimeter as the curve will enclose the maximum feasible area for any closed curve enclosing a region. No other form can include as much space around a set boundary. This thesis presents a comprehensive proof of the isoperimetric inequality in the Euclidean plane (R^2). The proof relies on the Fourier analysis-based Wirtinger inequality. By reparameterizing an arbitrary curve on ([-1,1]) and applying Wirtinger, the inequality is shown to hold for smooth curves. A density argument extends the conclusion to all finite-length Sobolev curves. The equality case precisely corresponds to circular curves. Applications like deriving explicit a priori PDE estimates and bounding ellipse parameters are explored, demonstrating the inequality’s utility beyond circles. It highlights the inequality’s theoretical significance while exploring practical uses in mathematics and physics. The journey elucidates deep connections between geometry and analysis via an elegant isoperimetric constraint.

In this Thesis we discuss the formation, foundation and application of Optimal Transport. We explore the motivation for the founding of the field and how it evolves into a widely applicable area of mathematics.
To consolidate the content of this thesis we explore an example of the primal use of Optimal Transport - logistics. In this example we consider Royal Air Force Lossiemouth. In our problem we must find the cheapest was of supplying the base with enough aviation fuel in order to maintain it’s operational capabilities as a base. We have three transport methods available to us and four other Royal Air force bases to supply the required fuel. This is done by setting up a Partial Optimal Transport problem and using Python code to find a solution numerically.
Our findings suggest that all fuel from the selected Royal Air Force stations to RAF Lossiemouth should be moved via Tanker Truck, which coincides with the cheaper option.










Why study mathematics if it cannot prove everything? Life after Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem


University of Hull, UK


2024/25


AbsURL



This dissertation explores the enduring nature of mathematics following the revelation of Godel’s first Incompleteness Theorem. It provides the building blocks required to construct a formal proof of the theorem, complete with examples of key concepts along the way. The inherent difference between truth and provability is carefully considered; both mathematically and philosophically. Following the proof, a discussion into life after Godel’s publication is carried out. The rebuttal of Wittgenstein; as well as the work of other philosophers was considered. This dissertation mirrors Camus’ approach to the absurd by considering the notion of mathematical suicide: a metaphor for the existential crisis following the collapse of Hilbert’s formalist dream. The development of computational theory from incompleteness is investigated through the Halting Problem, before considering the current P vs NP problem. Then, by examining the nature of uncertainty in quantum mechanics, and the Axiom of Choice and Continuum Hypothesis alongside Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, this dissertation proposes a new visualisation for the structure of a mathematical universe. Finally, the title question is answered by arguing that incompleteness is not a failure of mathematics, it is a feature. Whilst its discovery means that consideration must be made when forming systems, it resonates with the human existential dialogue with the uncertain, making mathematics more alive than ever.
